Town planningCitadel and lower townDrainage systemStandardisation

The Harappan Civilization (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE) was India's first urban culture, the Bronze Age "first urbanisation". Excavations at Harappa (Daya Ram Sahni, 1921), Mohenjo-daro (R.D. Banerji, 1922), Kalibangan, Lothal, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi reveal a remarkable degree of civic planning: planned streets, standard bricks, covered drains and public buildings, spread over a vast area, yet without any clearly identified palace or temple.

1. Layout of the city

  • Grid pattern: main streets ran north–south and east–west, crossing at right angles and dividing the town into rectangular blocks; narrow lanes led into the residential quarters.
  • Two-part division: a raised, fortified citadel on the west held public buildings, while a larger lower town on the east housed the people. Dholavira had a three-fold division into citadel, middle town and lower town.
  • Zoning of activities: bead-making workshops at Lothal and Chanhudaro and circular working floors near the granaries of Harappa suggest planned use of space.

2. Buildings and materials

  • Standardised bricks: burnt bricks in the uniform ratio 1:2:4 were used across a huge area, showing common standards of measurement; Kalibangan used mud bricks and Dholavira mainly stone.
  • Houses: one or two storeys built around courtyards, with wells, bathrooms and kitchens; doors opened into side lanes rather than main streets, ensuring privacy.
  • Public structures: the Great Bath (about 12 m × 7 m × 2.4 m) at Mohenjo-daro, made watertight with a layer of bitumen; granaries at Harappa; the dockyard at Lothal; and the stone reservoirs of Dholavira.

3. Sanitation and water management

  • Covered drainage: house drains joined brick-lined street drains with manholes and soak pits, among the most advanced systems of the Bronze Age world.
  • Water supply: Mohenjo-daro had several hundred wells, while Dholavira stored rain and stream water in a chain of rock-cut reservoirs in the dry Kutch region.
  • Civic discipline: regular cleaning of drains and disposal of refuse imply some form of municipal authority.

4. A critical view

  • Uniformity exaggerated: Lothal had a single enclosing wall, Kalibangan fortified both parts and Banawali's streets were not on a grid, so there was no single template.
  • Debated functions: whether the "granary" was a granary or an assembly hall, and the "dockyard" a dock or a water tank, is still discussed.
  • Decline: in the late phase, houses at Mohenjo-daro encroached on streets and building quality fell, showing weakening civic control.
  • Unknown authority: with no palaces or royal tombs, it is unclear whether priests, merchants or a council planned and enforced civic rules.

Harappan planning thus combined standardisation, sanitation and zoning on a scale unmatched in its age, even if it was less uniform than once believed. Dholavira's inscription as a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2021) shows its global value, and its water harvesting and drainage still offer lessons for planned cities such as Amaravati.
free.g1m-2020-p2-2b:
BhaktiSaguna and nirgunaVernacular literatureSocial equality

The Bhakti movement began with the Alvars and Nayanars of the Tamil country (6th–9th centuries) and spread across India between the 12th and 17th centuries through saints such as Ramanuja, Basavanna, Kabir, Nanak, Chaitanya and Tukaram. It preached personal devotion to God as the path to salvation, cutting across caste, gender and ritual, and left a deep imprint on religion, society and culture.

1. Religious impact

  • Simplified religion: devotion, the guru and the chanting of God's name replaced costly rituals and priestly mediation, bringing religion within reach of ordinary people.
  • Two streams: saguna saints such as Tulsidas, Surdas and Mirabai worshipped Rama or Krishna, while nirguna saints such as Kabir and Guru Nanak stressed one formless God; Nanak's teachings gave rise to Sikhism.
  • Composite culture: interaction with Sufi orders such as the Chishtis promoted Hindu–Muslim understanding; Kabir's dohas are revered by both communities.

2. Social impact

  • Challenge to caste: saints came from all castes, such as Kabir (weaver), Ravidas (leather worker) and Namdev (tailor), and Basavanna's Virashaivism rejected caste and ritual.
  • Space for women: Andal, Akka Mahadevi, Lal Ded and Mirabai found spiritual expression and defied social convention.
  • Collective worship: the langar of the Sikh Gurus and Sankardev's namghars in Assam encouraged worship and dining across caste lines.

3. Literary and cultural impact

  • Regional languages flowered: saints wrote in the people's languages rather than Sanskrit, creating lasting classics (see table).
  • Music and dance: bhajans, kirtans and abhangs enriched devotional music, and Siddhendra Yogi's Bhama Kalapam shaped Kuchipudi.
  • Shared identities: pilgrimages such as the Warkari yatra to Pandharpur created a common regional culture across castes.

4. In Andhra

  • Devotional literature: Annamacharya's thousands of sankirtanas, Bammera Potana's Telugu Bhagavatam and Bhadrachala Ramadasu's keertanas carried devotion to the masses.
  • Voice of protest: Vemana's verses and Pothuluri Veerabrahmam's Kalagnanam attacked caste, idol worship and superstition in simple Telugu.

5. Limitations

  • Caste survived: the caste system was not dismantled, and many sects later became ritualistic and caste-based themselves.
  • Limited change for women: the status of women in society changed little outside the devotional sphere.
  • Non-political: the movement largely accepted the existing social and political order.

The Bhakti movement thus democratised religion, enriched vernacular culture and spread the values of equality and tolerance that the Constitution later embodied; its legacy of composite culture remains a resource for social harmony.
free.g1m-2020-p2-3a:
Centralised bureaucracyMansabdariDivision of powersSulh-i-kul

Akbar (1556–1605) built a centralised, bureaucratic administration, described in Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari, which became the model for later Mughal rule. Its core was an emperor with wide powers, a group of ministers with divided functions, and the mansabdari system that bound the nobility to the throne. The system was efficient, but it also depended heavily on the ability of the ruler.

1. The Emperor

  • Supreme authority: the emperor was the head of the state, the army and justice, and the final court of appeal.
  • Theory of kingship: Abul Fazl described kingship as a divine light (farr-i-izidi) and stressed the ruler's duty to all subjects; sulh-i-kul (peace with all) guided state policy.
  • Religious authority: the Mahzar (1579) strengthened Akbar's authority in religious matters, while the abolition of the pilgrim tax (1563) and jizya (1564) won the loyalty of non-Muslim subjects.

2. Ministers: division of power

  • Reduced Wakil: earlier the all-powerful regent (Bairam Khan), the Wakil became largely an honorific post, so that no single minister could dominate.
  • Diwan (Wazir): head of revenue and finance; under Raja Todar Mal the zabti or dahsala system (1580) assessed revenue on the average produce and prices of the previous ten years.
  • Mir Bakhshi: head of the military department, responsible for mansabdari appointments, branding of horses (dagh) and descriptive rolls (chehra); news-writers reported to him.
  • Other ministers: each had a separate department, so power was balanced among them (see table).

3. Mansabdari and provinces

  • Mansabdari: every officer held a numerical rank with zat (personal rank and pay) and sawar (number of horsemen), combining civil and military duties; ranks were not hereditary.
  • Jagirs: most mansabdars were paid through jagirs (revenue assignments), which were transferred frequently so that no noble could build a local base.
  • Uniform provinces: in 1580 the empire was divided into twelve subas, each with a subedar, diwan, bakhshi, sadr, qazi and kotwal; the provincial diwan reported to the central diwan, a check on the governor.

4. Critical evaluation

  • Strengths: checks and balances among ministers, a service open to talent, integration of Rajputs, Iranis, Turanis and Indian Muslims, and a sound, data-based revenue system.
  • Weaknesses: an autocracy dependent on the ruler's personality, a costly mansabdari system, officials distant from the people because of frequent transfers, and later abuse that produced the jagirdari crisis.

AP angle: The Qutb Shahis of Golconda ruled Andhra independently until Aurangzeb annexed Golconda in 1687; Mughal institutions such as the mansabdari system were then extended to the region.

Akbar's administration blended Persian, Central Asian and Indian traditions into a durable structure that held the empire together for over a century, though its strength rested heavily on the personality of the emperor.

Hindavi SwarajyaGuerrilla warfareAshtapradhanChauth and sardeshmukhi

The Marathas rose in the 17th century from soldiers and feudatories of the Deccan Sultanates to an independent kingdom under Shivaji (1630–1680), and later to a pan-Indian power under the Peshwas. Shivaji turned favourable geography, a regional identity shaped by the Bhakti saints and the weakness of the Sultanates into a sovereign Hindavi Swarajya with a strong army and a sound administration.

1. Factors behind the rise

  • Geography: the rugged Sahyadris, deep valleys and hill forts suited guerrilla warfare by light cavalry against large Mughal and Bijapuri armies.
  • Cultural unity: Bhakti saints such as Eknath, Tukaram and Ramdas preached devotion and equality in Marathi, creating a shared regional identity.
  • Experience: Maratha chiefs such as Shahji Bhonsle had gained military and administrative experience in the service of Ahmednagar and Bijapur.
  • Political vacuum: the decline of the Deccan Sultanates and the pressure of Mughal expansion stirred regional resistance.

2. Shivaji's military and political career

  • Early conquests: starting with Torna (1646), he built a base of forts around the Pune jagir, killed Afzal Khan of Bijapur at Pratapgarh (1659), raided Shaista Khan's camp at Pune (1663) and sacked Surat (1664).
  • Setback and recovery: the Treaty of Purandar (1665) with Raja Jai Singh cost him 23 forts, but after escaping from Agra (1666) he recovered his territories.
  • Sovereignty: his coronation at Raigad (1674) as Chhatrapati gave legitimacy to an independent kingdom.

3. Administration

  • Ashtapradhan: a council of eight ministers advised the king, each with a defined department; under Shivaji these posts were neither hereditary nor permanent.
  • Revenue: land was surveyed and assessed, and revenue was collected by state officials; Shivaji preferred cash salaries to jagirs to curb the power of local chiefs.
  • Chauth and sardeshmukhi: one-fourth and an additional one-tenth of the revenue were levied on neighbouring territories in return for protection from raids.
  • Army, forts and navy: a mobile light cavalry, a chain of forts under officers of different castes, and a navy with sea forts such as Sindhudurg.
  • Religious tolerance: he respected places of worship of all faiths and employed Muslims in his army and navy.

4. Critical note

  • Burden of raids: chauth raids and the sack of Surat caused hardship in neighbouring regions.
  • Fragile unity: the later Maratha confederacy lacked unity and suffered a major setback at Panipat (1761).

AP angle: In his Karnataka expedition (1677–78), Shivaji allied with Abul Hasan Qutb Shah of Golconda and his ministers Madanna and Akkanna, who helped finance the campaign.

Shivaji's swarajya laid the foundation of the Maratha empire, which under the Peshwas became the strongest Indian power of the 18th century; his blend of guerrilla warfare, forts and administrative discipline remains his lasting legacy.
free.g1m-2020-p2-4a:
Subsidiary AllianceLord WellesleyParamountcyCeded Districts

The Subsidiary Alliance was devised by Lord Wellesley (Governor-General, 1798–1805), building on Dupleix's practice of lending troops to Indian rulers. It let the East India Company control Indian states without costly wars, by making them pay for British troops stationed in their own territory. Between 1798 and 1818 it became a main instrument by which the British established paramountcy in India.

1. Main features

  • Subsidiary force: the ruler had to accept a British force within his territory and pay for its upkeep in cash or by ceding territory.
  • Resident: a British Resident was stationed at his court and gradually became the real power behind the throne.
  • Foreign policy surrendered: the ruler could not employ other Europeans, especially the French, or make war or alliances without British consent.
  • Promise of protection: in return, the Company guaranteed protection against external attack and internal revolt and promised non-interference in internal affairs, a promise rarely kept.

2. Role in British expansion

  • An army at Indian expense: the Company maintained a large army paid for by Indian states and stationed it at strategic points.
  • Elimination of rivals: control of the states' foreign policy removed French influence and isolated the Marathas; the Treaty of Bassein (1802) with Peshwa Baji Rao II drew the Company into the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
  • Territorial gains: Awadh ceded about half its territory (Rohilkhand and the Doab) in 1801, greatly enlarging British India.
  • Disarming the states: with their armies disbanded, the states could not resist later British demands.

AP angle: In 1800 the Nizam ceded the districts he had acquired from Mysore (Bellary and Cuddapah) to pay for the subsidiary force. These Ceded Districts came under Thomas Munro, who introduced the ryotwari system there, so part of present Rayalaseema came under direct British rule through this alliance.

3. Critical view

  • Loss of sovereignty: states lost their independence, and soldiers of their disbanded armies swelled the ranks of the Pindaris.
  • Financial ruin: the subsidy drained state finances, and arrears became an excuse for demanding more territory.
  • Misgovernance: protected from rebellion, rulers neglected governance, which was later used to justify annexation (Awadh, 1856).
  • One instrument among many: wars against Mysore and the Marathas, and later the Doctrine of Lapse, also drove expansion.

By 1818 the Subsidiary Alliance had turned most Indian states into dependencies and made the British the paramount power in India. It was a classic case of conquest by treaty, paid for by the conquered themselves.

Depressed classesMahad SatyagrahaPoona PactLabour welfare

Dr. B.R. Ambedkar (1891–1956), born into the Mahar community, overcame caste discrimination to earn doctorates from Columbia University and the London School of Economics. He became the foremost leader of the depressed classes and a champion of labour rights in colonial India, arguing that political freedom was meaningless without social and economic democracy.

1. Awakening and organising the untouchables

  • Organisation: the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924) worked for the education and uplift of the depressed classes, and the People's Education Society (1945) opened colleges for them.
  • Press: his journals Mooknayak (1920) and Bahishkrit Bharat (1927) gave voice to their grievances and built self-respect.
  • Ideas: Annihilation of Caste (1936) argued that caste must be destroyed, not reformed, because it rested on scriptural sanction.

2. Direct action against untouchability

  • Mahad Satyagraha (1927): asserted the right of untouchables to draw water from the public Chavdar tank.
  • Burning of the Manusmriti (1927): a public rejection of the scriptural basis of caste inequality.
  • Kalaram temple satyagraha (Nashik, 1930): demanded the right of temple entry.

3. Political rights

  • Representation: he represented the depressed classes at the Round Table Conferences, and the Communal Award (1932) gave them separate electorates.
  • Poona Pact (1932): after Gandhi's fast, separate electorates were given up for 148 reserved seats in provincial legislatures under joint electorates.
  • Own platform: the Scheduled Castes Federation (1942) gave the depressed classes an independent political voice.

4. For labourers

  • Independent Labour Party (1936): fought for workers and tenants; he opposed the khoti system of landlordism in Konkan and the Bombay Industrial Disputes Bill (1938) that restricted strikes.
  • Labour Member (1942–46): in the Viceroy's Executive Council he laid the foundations of Indian labour law (see diagram).

Critical assessment: His demand for separate electorates clashed with the Congress view of national unity, and his early base was largely in Maharashtra. Yet he made caste a political question and gave the depressed classes self-respect.

AP angle: In Andhra, the same struggle found expression in Gurram Jashuva's Gabbilam (1941) and in later Dalit movements inspired by Ambedkar.

His vision was embedded in the Constitution: Article 17 (abolition of untouchability), Articles 15–16, Article 46, and labour provisions in Articles 23, 24, 42 and 43, making social democracy a constitutional goal.

Cabinet MissionGrouping of provincesConstituent AssemblyInterim Government

The Cabinet Mission of Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander was sent by the Attlee government and reached India in March 1946. Failing to bring the Congress and the Muslim League to agreement, it announced its own plan on 16 May 1946 to transfer power to a united India through a loose federation, a Constituent Assembly and an interim government.

1. A united India with a weak centre

  • No sovereign Pakistan: the Mission rejected a fully sovereign Pakistan, as it would leave large non-Muslim minorities within it.
  • Limited Union: a Union of India, including British provinces and princely states, would deal only with defence, foreign affairs and communications and raise the necessary finances.
  • Strong provinces: all residuary powers would rest with the provinces and states.

2. Grouping of provinces

  • Three sections: provinces would form three groups, and each group could frame a constitution for its provinces (see table).
  • Exit option: a province could leave its group after the first general election, and the constitution could be reviewed after ten years.

3. Constituent Assembly and interim government

  • Constituent Assembly: 389 members (292 from provinces, 4 from Chief Commissioner's provinces and 93 from princely states), elected indirectly by provincial assemblies at about one seat per million population, divided among General, Muslim and Sikh communities.
  • Interim government: Indian leaders would hold all portfolios until the new constitution came into force.
  • Princely states: paramountcy would lapse with the transfer of power.

4. Outcome and evaluation

  • Dispute over grouping: both parties initially accepted the plan, but the League saw grouping as compulsory and the Congress as optional. After Nehru's statement of July 1946, the League withdrew and called for Direct Action (16 August 1946), which triggered communal riots.
  • Assembly elections (July 1946): the Congress won 208 seats, the League 73 and others 15.
  • Institutions born: the Interim Government under Nehru took office on 2 September 1946 (the League joined in October), and the Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946.
  • Andhra in the Assembly: leaders such as T. Prakasam, N.G. Ranga, Pattabhi Sitaramayya and Durgabai Deshmukh entered it from Madras.

Assessment: The plan's weak centre and ambiguous grouping clause were its fatal flaws. It failed to prevent Partition, but it gave India the Constituent Assembly that framed the Constitution, and its federal ideas influenced later debates.

Quit IndiaDo or DieMass upsurgeParallel governments

On 8 August 1942 the AICC session at Gowalia Tank, Bombay, passed the Quit India resolution, and Gandhi gave the call "Do or Die". The failure of the Cripps Mission, the Japanese advance towards India, wartime shortages and rising prices led to this final mass struggle. Though crushed within months, it changed the course of the freedom movement.

1. Course of the movement

  • Spontaneous revolt: with leaders in jail, people struck at symbols of authority: strikes, attacks on railways, telegraph lines and police stations.
  • Underground network: Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia and Aruna Asaf Ali led underground work, and Usha Mehta ran the Congress Radio.
  • Parallel governments: set up in Ballia, Tamluk and Satara (see table).

2. Positive impact

  • Independence non-negotiable: after the war, the only question was how power would be transferred, not whether.
  • Mass participation: students, workers, peasants and women joined in unprecedented numbers, and the youth were radicalised.
  • British realisation: the Viceroy Linlithgow called it the most serious rebellion since 1857; India could not be held for long against the will of its people.
  • Moral stature: Gandhi's 21-day fast (1943) in detention kept the national spirit alive.
  • Leadership from below: with top leaders in jail, socialists, students and local leaders took the initiative, showing how deeply nationalism had spread.

3. Limitations

  • Suppressed by force: tens of thousands were arrested and the Congress was banned; the mass phase was crushed within months, though underground activity continued.
  • No immediate gain: the British conceded nothing during the war.
  • Violence: widespread violence departed from Gandhian non-violence.
  • Divisions: the Muslim League, the Communists (with their "People's War" line), the Hindu Mahasabha and the princely states stayed away; the League gained ground while Congress leaders were in jail.

4. In Andhra

  • Andhra circular: the Andhra PCC's circular of 29 July 1942 (the "Andhra" or "Kurnool" circular) urged defiance of orders, cutting of telegraph wires and non-payment of taxes.
  • Tenali and Guntur: on 12 August crowds set fire to part of Tenali railway station and police firing killed several protesters (the Tenali martyrs); students were fired upon at Guntur.

Thus, though crushed by force, the Quit India Movement was a decisive moral and political blow that made independence only a matter of time; it remains the high point of mass nationalism.
free.g1m-2020-p2-6a:
Agrarian expansionLand grantsBhagaKrishna–Godavari delta

The Satavahanas (c. 1st century BCE to 3rd century CE), the first great Andhra dynasty, ruled the Deccan from Pratishthana and Dhanyakataka (Amaravati). The Nasik, Karle and Naneghat inscriptions and Hala's Gathasaptasati reveal a well-developed agrarian economy that supported towns, Buddhist monasteries and Roman trade, and introduced the practice of land grants.

1. Crops and techniques

  • Rice bowl: the Krishna–Godavari deltas formed a great rice-growing region, while cotton (Andhra cotton was noted in foreign accounts), millets, pulses and sugarcane were grown elsewhere.
  • Better techniques: iron ploughshares and paddy transplantation raised output.
  • Irrigation: tanks, wells and cisterns supported cultivation; inscriptions record donations of wells by pious individuals.

2. Land ownership and labour

  • Crown and private land: the king held crown lands, while gahapatis (householders) and kutumbikas (cultivating families) held private land.
  • Labour: halikas (ploughmen) and hired labourers worked the fields of the larger landholders.
  • Village life: Hala's Gathasaptasati portrays farming villages, festivals and rural life in Prakrit verse.

3. Revenue and administration

  • Bhaga: the king's share, traditionally one-sixth of the produce, was collected in cash and kind, besides dues on salt and other items.
  • Measurement: land was measured in nivartanas.
  • Administrative units: the ahara (district) was under an amatya and the village under a gramika, who looked after revenue and order.

4. Land grants

  • First of their kind: the Satavahanas were the first rulers to grant tax-free villages to Brahmanas and Buddhist monks; Gautamiputra Satakarni's Nasik grants are examples.
  • Immunities: royal troops and officials could not enter the granted land, and it could not be dug for salt, a royal monopoly.
  • Agrarian frontier: grants carried cultivation into forest areas and spread Brahmanical and Buddhist culture.

5. Links with trade

  • Surplus for exchange: agrarian surplus fed Roman trade and craft guilds (srenis), which also acted as banks accepting permanent deposits.
  • Money economy: Satavahana lead and copper coins, including ship-type coins, show the commercialisation of agrarian products.
  • Agrarian towns: the surplus sustained urban centres such as Dhanyakataka and Pratishthana, and the ports of the Krishna–Godavari coast exported rice, cotton and textiles.

Assessment: Land grants extended cultivation, but by transferring revenue and administrative rights they planted the seeds of feudalism, as R.S. Sharma argues. The Satavahana agrarian base sustained the Amaravati Buddhist culture and shaped Andhra's village economy for centuries.

Dravida styleRock-cut mandapasMonolithic rathasStructural temples

The Pallavas (c. 3rd–9th century CE) ruled from Kanchipuram; their earliest Prakrit charters, such as the Mayidavolu plates of Shivaskandavarman found in Guntur district, show their early hold over the Krishna region of Andhra. Their greatest legacy is art: they carried South Indian architecture from rock-cut caves to structural stone temples and laid the foundation of the Dravida style perfected by the Cholas.

1. Stages of evolution

  • Mahendra style: Mahendravarman I began rock-cut cave temples (mandapas) with pillared halls; the Mandagapattu inscription calls his shrine a temple built without brick, timber, metal or mortar.
  • Mamalla style: Narasimhavarman I Mamalla created the monolithic rathas at Mahabalipuram, each carved from a single rock to imitate a different building form, and cave mandapas such as the Mahishasuramardini and Varaha.
  • Rajasimha style: Narasimhavarman II built structural stone temples such as the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram, with pyramidal vimanas.
  • Later Pallava style: Nandivarman II and his successors built temples such as Vaikuntha Perumal at Kanchipuram, whose sculptured panels narrate Pallava history.

2. Sculpture and painting

  • Open-air relief: the great relief at Mahabalipuram, the "Descent of the Ganga" or "Arjuna's Penance", shows gods, sages, elephants and even a mock-ascetic cat with lively realism.
  • Narrative panels: the Mahishasuramardini panel shows the goddess fighting the buffalo demon, and Somaskanda panels (Shiva with Uma and Skanda) adorn the sanctum walls of Rajasimha's temples.
  • Painting and patronage: traces of murals survive in the Kailasanatha temple; Mahendravarman I bore the title Chitrakarapuli and wrote the Sanskrit farce Mattavilasa Prahasana.

3. Andhra link

  • Early base: the early Pallavas issued charters in the Krishna–Guntur region before Kanchipuram became their centre.
  • Influence: the rock-cut cave temples at Bhairavakonda (Nellore district) show Pallava influence on Andhra's rock architecture.

4. Legacy

  • Prototype for the Cholas: the tiered pyramidal vimana led to great Chola temples such as the Brihadeeswara at Thanjavur.
  • Wider influence: the Kailasanatha temple influenced the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal, built under the Chalukyas of Badami, and the Pallava Grantha script spread to Southeast Asia.
  • World heritage: the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1984).

The Pallavas thus carried Indian temple architecture from rock-cut caves to structural stone temples, combining engineering skill with naturalistic sculpture and laying the foundation of the Dravida tradition of South India.
free.g1m-2020-p2-7b:
Literary renaissanceRoyal patronagePrabandhaAshtadiggajas

The Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka, traditionally with the guidance of Vidyaranya. The same age saw a vigorous revival of Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada and Tamil literature, culminating in the golden age of Telugu under Krishnadevaraya. The statement is therefore largely valid, though the literary movement had roots that were older than the empire.

1. Sanskrit

  • Vedic and philosophical works: Sayana's commentaries on the Vedas and Vidyaranya's Advaita works appeared under the early Sangamas.
  • Court literature: Gangadevi's Madhuravijayam described her husband Kumara Kampana's conquest of Madurai, and Krishnadevaraya wrote the Sanskrit drama Jambavati Kalyanam.

2. Telugu

  • Early patronage: Nachana Somana (Uttara Harivamsam) was honoured by Bukka I, and Srinatha, poet of the Reddi courts, defeated the scholar Dindima Bhatta in debate at the court of Devaraya II and was honoured with a kanakabhishekam (bath of gold coins).
  • Devotional poetry: Tallapaka Annamacharya composed thousands of Telugu sankirtanas on Lord Venkateswara in this age.
  • The golden age: Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529), hailed as Andhra Bhoja, wrote Amuktamalyada and declared "Desa bhashalandu Telugu lessa" (Telugu is the finest of the regional languages).
  • Prabandha: the Ashtadiggajas, eight poets traditionally associated with his court, perfected the prabandha; Allasani Peddana's Manucharitra earned him the title Andhra Kavitapitamaha.

3. Kannada and Tamil

  • Kannada: Kumaravyasa's Karnata Bharata Kathamanjari, and the Haridasa saints Purandaradasa and Kanakadasa, whose songs enriched Carnatic music.
  • Tamil: Villiputturar's Tamil Mahabharatam and Arunagirinathar's Tiruppugazh.

4. Why the two coincided

  • Royal patronage: kings presented themselves as protectors of dharma and culture and rewarded poets with land and honours.
  • Prosperity: wealth from trade and agriculture supported temples and mathas such as Sringeri, which acted as centres of learning.
  • Bhakti and regional languages: devotional movements took literature to the people in their own languages.

5. Critical view

  • Older roots: Nannaya and Tikkana had written earlier, and the Reddi courts ran parallel, with Errana completing the Telugu Mahabharata under Prolaya Vema Reddi.
  • Limits of the prabandha: later prabandhas were criticised for ornate style, erotic themes and courtly imitation, and the movement declined after 1565.

Vijayanagara's political revival and the literary renaissance thus reinforced each other, giving Telugu its finest classical age and leaving a multilingual legacy shared by the whole of South India.
free.g1m-2020-p2-8a:
Grandhalaya movementTelugu renaissanceAdult educationPublic libraries Act

The library movement (Grandhalaya Udyamam) in Andhra was part of the Telugu renaissance and the national awakening. It aimed to spread literacy, Telugu literature and political consciousness by setting up public libraries, reading rooms and night schools in towns and villages. Led by Iyyanki Venkata Ramanaiah, it made Andhra a pioneer of the public library idea in India.

1. Origins

  • Early libraries: the library started by Nalam Krishna Rao at Rajahmundry in 1898, which later merged with the Vasuraya library to form the Gowthami Grandhalayam; the Sri Krishnadevaraya Andhra Bhasha Nilayam, Hyderabad (1901), founded with the help of Komarraju Venkata Lakshmana Rao; and the Rammohan Library, Vijayawada.
  • Swadeshi impetus: the Vandemataram movement (1905) gave the movement energy, and libraries became places for reading newspapers and discussing national issues.

2. Organisation and leaders

  • Andhra Desa Grandhalaya Sangham: formed on 10 April 1914 at Vijayawada at the first Andhra library conference, presided over by Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham.
  • Iyyanki Venkata Ramanaiah: its secretary from 1914 to 1939, he started library training classes and organised the All India Public Library Conference at Madras (1919).
  • Grandhalaya Sarvaswam: its journal is regarded as India's first library journal in an Indian language.
  • Innovators: Paturi Nagabhushanam started boat libraries on the Krishna canals in Guntur district (1935); Vavilala Gopalakrishnaiah was another leading figure.

3. Features and methods

  • Village reading rooms: libraries were set up by villagers themselves, often with donated books and newspapers.
  • Adult education: night schools, lectures and conferences spread literacy among adults.
  • Mobilisation: library conferences and "library pilgrimages" carried the message from village to village.

4. Impact

  • Political awakening: libraries spread nationalism and fed the Andhra movement; in Telangana, they supported the Telugu cultural awakening under the Nizam's restrictions.
  • Language and literature: they popularised modern Telugu prose, newspapers and books among ordinary readers.
  • Social mixing: reading rooms brought people of different castes and classes together and spread reformist ideas.
  • Legislation: the movement led to the Madras Public Libraries Act, 1948 (the first in India) and the Andhra Pradesh Public Libraries Act, 1960, which created Zilla Grandhalaya Samsthas funded by a library cess.

The library movement treated knowledge as a public good; today, district library networks and digital libraries carry this legacy forward and can bridge the digital divide in rural Andhra Pradesh.
free.g1m-2020-p2-8b:
Telugu renaissanceWidow remarriageWomen's educationReform through literature

Kandukuri Veeresalingam Pantulu (1848–1919) of Rajahmundry, hailed as the father of the Telugu Renaissance and "Gadya Tikkana", led the social reform movement in Andhra in the late 19th century. Influenced by the Brahmo Samaj and Western liberal thought, he combined writing, journalism and direct action to fight widow remarriage bans, child marriage and superstition.

1. Reform of women's condition

  • Widow remarriage: he performed the first widow remarriage in Andhra at Rajahmundry on 11 December 1881, organised many more and set up a home for widows; the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856 gave these marriages legal backing.
  • Women's education: he started a girls' school at Dowleswaram (1874) and published Satihitabodhini, a journal for women.
  • Against social evils: he campaigned against child marriage, kanyasulkam (bride-price), the nautch system and superstition.

2. Press and institutions

  • Vivekavardhini (1874): his journal exposed corruption among officials and the hypocrisy of orthodoxy.
  • Hitakarini Samajam (1906): he donated his property to this society to continue his reform work after him.
  • Reform network: his associates and students carried reform to other towns of coastal Andhra.

3. Literature as a weapon

  • First Telugu novel: Rajasekhara Charitramu, modelled on Goldsmith's The Vicar of Wakefield, satirised superstition and gullibility.
  • New genres: he wrote the first Telugu autobiography, satirical plays (prahasanas) and a history of Telugu poets (Andhra Kavula Charitramu).
  • Simple prose: he used plain Telugu prose that common readers could understand.

4. Critical evaluation

  • Strengths: he institutionalised reform in Andhra for the first time and inspired reformers and writers such as Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu and Gurajada Apparao.
  • Limitations: the movement largely remained within upper-caste, urban and English-educated circles, gave less attention to untouchability and caste, and relied on colonial law and authority.
  • Social cost: remarried couples faced social boycott from orthodox society, limiting the spread of reform.
  • Builder on others' work: he adapted the methods of reformers such as Vidyasagar in Bengal to Andhra conditions, but gave them a distinct Telugu literary voice.

On balance, Veeresalingam gave social reform in Andhra its direction, institutions and literary voice, paving the way for laws such as the Child Marriage Restraint Act (1929) and the constitutional promise of equality for women under Articles 14 and 15.
free.g1m-2020-p2-9a:
Non-Brahmin movementCommunal representationDravidian identityMontford Reforms

The South Indian Liberal Federation, popularly called the Justice Party after its English newspaper, was founded in Madras on 20 November 1916 by Dr. T.M. Nair, Sir P. Theagaraya Chetty and Dr. C. Natesa Mudaliar. It issued the Non-Brahmin Manifesto in December 1916. Its formation reflected social, cultural and political tensions in early 20th-century Madras Presidency.

1. Social circumstances

  • Brahmin dominance: a small Brahmin minority held a disproportionate share of higher education, government jobs, the judiciary, the press and politics, causing resentment among educated non-Brahmin elites.
  • Rising non-Brahmin elites: landholders, merchants and newly educated professionals sought a share in power matching their numbers and wealth.
  • Educational gap: English education had spread first and fastest among Brahmins, who therefore dominated the new professions and services created by colonial rule.

2. Cultural circumstances

  • Dravidian identity: Western education and scholarship such as Robert Caldwell's Comparative Grammar of the Dravidian languages (1856) fostered a separate Dravidian consciousness.
  • Early organisation: the Madras Dravidian Association (1912) preceded the party and voiced non-Brahmin grievances.

3. Political circumstances

  • Fear of Home Rule: the Congress and Annie Besant's Home Rule League were seen as Brahmin-led, and non-Brahmins feared that self-government would mean Brahmin rule.
  • Constitutional reforms: Montagu's declaration (1917) and the Montford Reforms prompted demands for communal representation; the Meston Award reserved 28 seats for non-Brahmins in Madras.
  • Colonial encouragement: the government encouraged the movement as a counterweight to nationalism.
  • Need for an organisation: non-Brahmin leaders realised that only an organised party with its own newspapers (Justice, Dravidan and Andhra Prakasika) could press these demands.

AP angle: Telugu zamindars and landholders were prominent; the Raja of Panagal and the Raja of Bobbili became Chief Ministers, and Andhra Prakasika was its Telugu paper.

4. Critical view

  • Achievements: it won the 1920 elections under dyarchy, aided by the Congress boycott, and introduced the Communal G.O. (1921) for reservations, the Hindu Religious Endowments Act and voting rights for women (1921).
  • Limitations: it was elitist and loyal to the British, stayed away from the freedom struggle and did little for the depressed classes.
  • Decline: it lost the 1937 elections and was transformed into the Dravidar Kazhagam under Periyar in 1944.

The Justice Party pioneered social justice through reservations, a principle later enshrined in Articles 15(4) and 16(4), even though its elitism and loyalism limited its role in the national movement.
free.g1m-2020-p2-9b:
Linguistic reorganisationPotti SreeramuluVisalandhraGentlemen's Agreement

Andhra State (1 October 1953) was the first state formed on a linguistic basis after independence, and Andhra Pradesh (1 November 1956) united the Telugu-speaking regions of Madras and Hyderabad States. Its formation was the climax of a half-century-old Andhra movement, set off by Potti Sreeramulu's sacrifice, and it changed India's federal map by making language the main basis of states.

1. Background before 1947

  • Andhra movement: the Andhra Mahasabha (first conference at Bapatla, 1913) demanded a separate Andhra province; the Congress created a separate Andhra PCC (1918) and accepted linguistic provinces at Nagpur (1920).
  • Regional unity: the Sribagh Pact (16 November 1937) reconciled Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema on the university, capital, High Court and irrigation.
  • Sense of neglect: Telugu people felt under-represented in jobs, education and irrigation within the composite Madras Presidency.

2. Delays after 1947

  • National unity first: after Partition, the Dar Commission (1948) and the JVP Committee (1949) advised postponing linguistic states.
  • Madras city dispute: the JVP Committee said Andhra could be formed if it gave up its claim to Madras city, which delayed agreement.

3. Andhra State, 1953

  • Sreeramulu's sacrifice: Potti Sreeramulu's fast for a separate state, begun on 19 October 1952, ended in his death on 15 December 1952 after 58 days, triggering widespread protests.
  • Formation: Nehru announced the formation of Andhra on 19 December 1952; after the Wanchoo Committee report, Andhra State was formed with Kurnool as capital and T. Prakasam as Chief Minister.
  • National impact: the success of the Andhra demand led to the appointment of the States Reorganisation Commission (1953).

4. Visalandhra and 1956

  • Visalandhra: the demand to unify the Telugu areas of Hyderabad State with Andhra gained strength, popularised especially by the Communists.
  • SRC view: the States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali, 1955) favoured a separate Telangana for the time being.
  • Compromise: the Gentlemen's Agreement (February 1956) promised safeguards for Telangana, and the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 created Andhra Pradesh with Hyderabad as capital and N. Sanjeeva Reddy as Chief Minister.

Critical view: The movement made linguistic reorganisation national policy, but unimplemented safeguards led to the Jai Telangana (1969) and Jai Andhra (1972) agitations, the Six-Point Formula and Article 371D (1973), and finally bifurcation in 2014.

Linguistic states have strengthened federalism without weakening national unity, provided regional aspirations and safeguards are honoured fairly.
free.g1m-2020-p2-12a:
High-yielding varietiesFood self-sufficiencyRegional disparityEvergreen Revolution

The Green Revolution refers to the sharp rise in foodgrain output from the mid-1960s through high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds, assured irrigation and chemical inputs. Globally pioneered by Norman Borlaug and in India led by M.S. Swaminathan, with C. Subramaniam as Agriculture Minister, it began with the HYV Programme in 1966-67, after the droughts of the mid-1960s exposed India's dependence on food imports.

1. Components

  • HYV seeds: Mexican dwarf wheat (Lerma Rojo 64, Sonora 64) and IR-8 rice from IRRI.
  • Inputs: irrigation from canals and tubewells, chemical fertilisers and pesticides.
  • Mechanisation: tractors, threshers and rural electrification.
  • Institutions: agricultural universities, ICAR research, cooperative credit, and the Food Corporation of India and Agricultural Prices Commission (both 1965) for procurement and minimum support prices.
  • Package approach: built on the Intensive Agricultural District Programme (1960-61), with Lal Bahadur Shastri's call of "Jai Jawan Jai Kisan" giving political backing.

2. Positive impacts

  • Food security: wheat output more than doubled between 1965-66 and 1971-72, ending dependence on PL-480 food imports; India produced over 350 million tonnes of foodgrains in 2024-25.
  • Rural prosperity: higher farm incomes, rural employment and agro-industries.
  • Welfare base: buffer stocks enabled the PDS and later the National Food Security Act (2013).

3. Negative impacts

  • Regional inequality: gains concentrated in Punjab, Haryana, western UP and irrigated deltas; rainfed areas were neglected.
  • Crop imbalance: wheat and rice gained while pulses, oilseeds and millets lagged.
  • Interpersonal inequality: large farmers gained more, and tenants were often evicted.
  • Ecological damage: groundwater depletion, soil salinity and nutrient imbalance, pesticide residues and loss of traditional varieties.
  • Costs and debt: costly seeds, fertilisers and pumps raised cultivation costs and farm indebtedness.

4. Correcting the imbalance

  • Eastern India: Bringing Green Revolution to Eastern India (BGREI, 2010-11) sought to extend gains to rice-growing eastern states.
  • Soil and water: Soil Health Cards (2015), micro-irrigation and balanced fertiliser use address nutrient imbalance and water stress.
  • Diversification: missions for pulses, oilseeds and millets aim to correct the cereal bias.

AP angle: The Godavari and Krishna deltas and the Nagarjuna Sagar command area became a rice bowl through HYV paddy. To reverse chemical overuse, AP now promotes the Community Managed Natural Farming programme (APCNF, launched 2016).

The way forward is Swaminathan's "Evergreen Revolution": higher productivity with ecological sustainability, crop diversification, extension of gains to eastern and rainfed India, and climate resilience.
free.g1m-2020-p2-12b:
Blue RevolutionSustainable fisheriesPMMSYAquaculture

Fisheries is a sunrise sector supporting the livelihoods of about 3 crore people. India is the third largest fish producer and second in aquaculture, with about 8% of global output; production reached 175.45 lakh tonnes in 2022-23, about three-fourths of it from inland fisheries. Managing this resource sustainably while raising fishers' incomes is the aim of India's Blue Revolution.

1. Fisheries management

  • Regulation: state Marine Fishing Regulation Acts, a uniform 61-day monsoon fishing ban in the EEZ (15 April–14 June on the east coast, 1 June–31 July on the west coast), and mesh-size and juvenile-catch norms protect breeding stocks.
  • Coastal aquaculture: the Coastal Aquaculture Authority Act, 2005 regulates shrimp farms to protect coastal land, water and mangroves.
  • Conservation: marine protected areas, artificial reefs, sea ranching and Coastal Regulation Zone rules protect India's EEZ of about 2.02 million sq km.
  • Science: CMFRI, CIFA, CIBA, the National Fisheries Development Board (2006) and INCOIS's potential fishing zone advisories guide sustainable harvest.

2. Development

  • Institutions: a separate Department of Fisheries (2019) under the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying.
  • Schemes: the Blue Revolution scheme (2015-16), the Fisheries and Aquaculture Infrastructure Development Fund (2018-19), the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY, 2020, ₹20,050 crore) and the PM Matsya Kisan Samridhi Sah-Yojana (2024).
  • Fishers' welfare: Kisan Credit Cards for fishers, insurance and relief during the ban period.
  • Infrastructure: fishing harbours, cold chains and deep-sea vessels to reduce post-harvest losses.
  • Exports: about ₹60,524 crore of marine products in 2023-24, led by frozen shrimp, with the USA as the largest market.

3. Issues

  • Overfishing: coastal waters are overexploited, with heavy bycatch of juveniles.
  • Ecological stress: pollution, loss of mangroves, disease in shrimp farms and climate change threaten stocks.
  • Conflicts and gaps: Indo-Sri Lanka fishing disputes and weak post-harvest infrastructure reduce fishers' incomes, while middlemen capture much of the value.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh is India's leading fish-producing state; its inland production of 45.06 lakh tonnes in 2022-23 was about a third of India's inland output, and it is the hub of shrimp aquaculture (Bhimavaram, Nellore). New fishing harbours are being developed at Juvvaladinne, Nizampatnam, Machilipatnam and Uppada.

A sustainable blue economy, balancing catch with conservation and fisher welfare, is the way forward.
free.g1m-2020-p2-14a:
Project TigerNTCAAll India Tiger EstimationLandscape conservation

Project Tiger was launched on 1 April 1973 with nine reserves covering about 14,000 sq km. It got statutory backing through the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) under the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2006. The All India Tiger Estimation (AITE) 2018, released on 29 July 2019, was the fourth cycle of national assessment and the best measure of the project's results.

1. Findings of AITE 2018

  • Numbers: 2,967 tigers (range 2,603–3,346), a 33% rise over 2,226 in 2014 and more than double the 1,411 of 2006; India met the St. Petersburg (2010) goal of doubling tigers four years before the 2022 deadline.
  • Leading states: Madhya Pradesh (526), Karnataka (524) and Uttarakhand (442); Andhra Pradesh had 48.
  • Method: recognised by Guinness World Records as the largest camera-trap wildlife survey.
  • Concerns: no tigers were recorded in the Buxa, Dampa and Palamau reserves, and numbers fell in Chhattisgarh.

2. Successes of Project Tiger

  • Recovery: steadily rising numbers and more reserves (50 in 2018, 58 by March 2025).
  • Protection: the Special Tiger Protection Force and better patrolling reduced poaching pressure.
  • Science: scientific monitoring (M-STrIPES) and Management Effectiveness Evaluation of reserves.
  • Umbrella species: protecting the tiger conserves whole ecosystems, watersheds and forest carbon.
  • Legal design: every reserve has an inviolate core (critical tiger habitat) and a buffer where people and wildlife coexist.
  • Global leadership: India launched the International Big Cat Alliance in 2023.

3. Shortcomings

  • Uneven success: gains are concentrated in a few landscapes, while several reserves hold very few tigers or none.
  • Carrying capacity: many reserves are close to saturation, so dispersing tigers move into farmland and villages.
  • Fragmentation: roads, railways and mines cut corridors between reserves.
  • Conflict: human–tiger conflict rises as tigers spill out of reserves.
  • Rights: tension between relocation of forest dwellers and the Forest Rights Act.

AP angle: The Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam Tiger Reserve, India's largest by area, anchors tiger conservation in the Nallamala; AP's count rose from 48 (2018) to 63 (2022).

Latest: AITE 2022 (released 2023) estimated an average of 3,682 tigers (minimum 3,167), about 75% of the world's wild tigers.

Project Tiger shows that science-based conservation works; the focus must now shift to corridors, coexistence with communities and landscape-level planning.
free.g1m-2020-p2-15a:
Environmental pollutionAnthropogenic factorsPollutantsPolluter pays

Environmental pollution is the presence in air, water or soil of substances in concentrations that harm living beings and the environment; the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 defines such substances as environmental pollutants. Pollution has natural causes, but in modern India it is driven mainly by anthropogenic factors linked to industry, cities, transport and farming.

1. Industrial and energy factors

  • Industrialisation: emissions and effluents from thermal power, chemical, pharmaceutical and cement units, and hazardous waste; accidents such as Bhopal (1984) and the LG Polymers styrene gas leak at Visakhapatnam (May 2020) show the risks.
  • Energy: heavy dependence on coal causes air pollution and fly-ash.
  • Mining and deforestation: cause soil erosion, dust and contamination of water.
  • Industrial clusters: the Central Pollution Control Board's Comprehensive Environmental Pollution Index identifies critically polluted industrial areas that need special action.

2. Urban and transport factors

  • Urbanisation: untreated sewage, solid and plastic waste, e-waste and construction dust.
  • Transport: vehicle exhaust releases particulate matter, nitrogen oxides and carbon monoxide.
  • Plastics: single-use plastics clog drains, choke animals and pollute rivers and the sea.
  • Household fuels: burning firewood and dung for cooking causes indoor air pollution in rural homes, which PM Ujjwala Yojana (2016) seeks to reduce.

3. Agricultural and social factors

  • Agriculture: overuse of fertilisers and pesticides causes eutrophication and soil degradation, and crop-residue burning pollutes the air.
  • Population and consumerism: rising demand and waste generation add to pressure on the environment.
  • Governance gaps: weak enforcement and low public awareness worsen the problem.

4. Natural factors

  • Natural events: volcanic eruptions, dust storms, forest fires and floods add pollutants, though their impact is smaller and temporary compared with human causes.

AP angle: Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada, Guntur and other AP cities are listed as non-attainment cities under the National Clean Air Programme; aquaculture ponds and effluents have degraded Kolleru lake, and pharma and industrial effluents affect coastal areas.

Responses: Articles 48A and 51A(g); the Water Act (1974), Air Act (1981) and Environment (Protection) Act (1986); the National Green Tribunal (2010); the National Clean Air Programme (2019); and the ban on identified single-use plastics (2022).

Applying the polluter-pays principle, a circular economy, cleaner technology and lifestyle change (Mission LiFE) are the way forward.
free.g1m-2020-p2-15b:
Sustainable developmentBrundtland ReportInter-generational equitySDGs

The Brundtland Commission's report "Our Common Future" (1987) defined sustainable development as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It balances economic growth with social equity and environmental protection, and today guides global policy through the Sustainable Development Goals.

1. Concept

  • Three pillars: economic growth, social equity and environmental protection must advance together.
  • Equity: inter-generational equity (fairness to future generations) and intra-generational equity (fairness among people today).
  • Principles: respect for the carrying capacity of ecosystems, and the precautionary and polluter-pays principles, recognised by the Supreme Court in Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum (1996).
  • Strong and weak sustainability: a debate over whether natural capital can be replaced by man-made capital, or must be conserved in its own right.

2. Global milestones

  • Evolution: from the Stockholm Conference (1972) to the Rio Earth Summit (1992, Agenda 21), the 2030 Agenda with 17 Sustainable Development Goals (2015) and the Paris Agreement (2015).

3. Importance

  • Finite resources: unchecked growth causes climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution.
  • Inclusive growth: sustainable development links poverty reduction, health, education and gender equality.
  • Economic resilience: renewable energy, resource efficiency and green jobs build long-term resilience.
  • Disaster risk reduction: it aids climate adaptation, vital for cyclone-prone coastal states.
  • Constitutional mandate: Article 21 (right to a clean environment), Article 48A and Article 51A(g).

4. India's efforts

  • Policies and targets: the National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008), Mission LiFE (2022) and the Panchamrit pledges at COP26 (2021), including 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070.
  • Clean energy: 50% of installed power capacity from non-fossil sources was achieved in 2025, five years ahead of the 2030 target.
  • Monitoring: NITI Aayog's SDG India Index tracks the progress of states.
  • Challenges: finance, technology and a just transition for workers in coal regions remain hurdles.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh is a Front Runner state in the SDG India Index 2023-24. Its Community Managed Natural Farming programme, the Kurnool Ultra Mega Solar Park, renewable energy and green hydrogen projects, and the Swarna Andhra@2047 vision aim to combine growth with sustainability.

Sustainable development is not a choice but a necessity; it calls for green growth, responsible consumption and people's participation.
free.g1m-2023-p2-1a:
Harappan continuityMaterial cultureProto-Hindu beliefsSubstratum of Indian civilization

The Harappan Civilization (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE) declined as a city culture, but it did not vanish. Its farming, crafts, beliefs and customs passed through Late Harappan and Chalcolithic village cultures into Vedic and later Indian life. Much of this inheritance survives today in villages, temples and households, so the Harappan world forms the substratum of Indian civilization rather than a dead past.

1. Town planning and technology

  • Planned settlements: grid-pattern streets, covered drains and soak pits at Mohenjodaro and Harappa anticipate the drainage and sanitation principles of modern town planning.
  • Water management: the reservoirs of Dholavira and the Great Bath foreshadow the stepwells and temple tanks of later India.
  • Weights and measures: cubical chert weights followed a binary system (1, 2, 4, 8, 16…); the 16-anna rupee, used until decimal coinage in 1957, follows the same logic.
  • Transport: terracotta models of bullock carts and boats closely resemble the carts and boats still used in Sindh, Rajasthan and Gujarat.

2. Economy and crafts

  • Agriculture: the criss-cross furrowed field at Kalibangan resembles the mixed cropping still practised in Rajasthan.
  • Cotton: the Harappans were among the earliest people to grow cotton; cotton textiles remain a hallmark of Indian craft.
  • Crafts: carnelian bead-making (still practised at Khambhat), black-on-red pottery and the potter's wheel continue in village crafts.

3. Religion and beliefs

  • Mother Goddess: numerous female figurines anticipate Shakti worship and village goddess cults.
  • Proto-Shiva: John Marshall read the 'Pashupati' seal, a horned figure in a yogic posture surrounded by animals, as proto-Shiva; linga–yoni stones point the same way.
  • Nature worship: the sacred pipal, the humped bull and the swastika remain objects of veneration.
  • Ritual: fire altars at Kalibangan and Lothal, and ritual bathing at the Great Bath, echo Vedic sacrifices and the Hindu emphasis on purificatory bathing.

4. Social customs and daily life

  • Ornaments: the bronze 'dancing girl' wears many bangles; red pigment in the hair-parting of figurines at Nausharo resembles sindoor (J.M. Kenoyer's interpretation).
  • Leisure and homes: dice, toy carts, whistles and courtyard houses with rooms opening inward survive in village life.

5. Limits of continuity

  • Lost elements: the script, standardised town planning and trade with Mesopotamia disappeared; cities returned only with the second urbanisation of the 6th century BCE.
  • Caveat: as the script is undeciphered, religious continuities are inferences from archaeology, not certainties.

AP angle: the mother-goddess cult lives on in AP's village goddesses (gramadevatas) such as Gangamma and Poleramma, and bullock carts and courtyard houses remain common in rural Andhra.

Thus Harappan culture survives less in monuments than in everyday practices, a striking example of continuity amid change in Indian civilization.
free.g1m-2023-p2-1b:
Chinese pilgrimsFa-Hien and Hiuen-TsangGupta and Harsha administrationBuddhist bias

Chinese Buddhist pilgrims came to India to visit the sacred places of the Buddha and to collect texts. Fa-Hien's Fo-kuo-ki (early 5th century), Hiuen-Tsang's Si-yu-ki (7th century) and I-Tsing's record of Buddhist practice (late 7th century) are dated, first-hand outsider sources on Gupta and post-Gupta India, though coloured by their Buddhist outlook.

1. Socio-religious life

  • Diet and customs (Fa-Hien): the people of Madhyadesha were prosperous; most avoided meat, liquor, onion and garlic, no pigs or fowls were kept, and cowries served as money in markets.
  • Untouchability: Fa-Hien saw Chandalas living outside towns and striking a piece of wood to announce their approach; Hiuen-Tsang found butchers, fishermen and scavengers living outside settlements, showing a hardening of caste.
  • Varna and learning (Hiuen-Tsang): he describes the four varnas and Brahmana vegetarianism, and Nalanda as a great centre with thousands of students, where he himself studied under Silabhadra.
  • Religion: Fa-Hien found Buddhism flourishing alongside Brahmanism; by Hiuen-Tsang's time Buddhism was declining in many regions. Harsha's quinquennial assembly at Prayag honoured the Buddha, Surya and Shiva.
  • Monastic life (I-Tsing): after about ten years at Nalanda, he described the vinaya discipline, the curriculum, Sanskrit grammar, medicine, diet and the hygiene of monks.

2. Administration

  • Gupta mildness (Fa-Hien): no registration of households; crimes were punished mostly by fines, with the cutting off of the right hand only for repeated rebellion; free hospitals and rest-houses existed at Pataliputra.
  • Harsha's revenue (Hiuen-Tsang): taxation was light, about one-sixth of the produce; revenue from crown lands was divided into four parts: for state affairs, for public servants, for scholars and for religious gifts.
  • Officials and labour: officials were paid by assignments of land, and forced labour was limited and paid.
  • Law and order: punishments were harsher than in Gupta times (mutilation and ordeals by water, fire, weighing and poison), and roads were unsafe; Hiuen-Tsang himself was robbed.

AP angle: Hiuen-Tsang visited Andhra (around Vengi) and Dhanakataka (the Amaravati region) and found many Buddhist monasteries, most of them deserted, evidence of Buddhism's decline in its old Andhra heartland.

3. Value and limitations

  • Value: precise dates and first-hand detail fill gaps in Indian texts; Hiuen-Tsang's descriptions later helped archaeologists identify Buddhist sites.
  • Limitations: a Buddhist bias, little political history, generalisations from short stays, and problems with Indian languages and names.

Read with inscriptions and Bana's Harshacharita, these accounts remain indispensable for reconstructing the society and governance of early India.
free.g1m-2025-p2-1a:
Harappan urbanismMehrgarhIndigenous originSpatial expansion

The Indus Valley or Harappan Civilization was South Asia's first urban culture, with a mature phase of about 2600–1900 BCE. It came to light when Daya Ram Sahni excavated Harappa (1921) and R.D. Banerji excavated Mohenjo-daro (1922). Planned cities, standard weights, seals and an undeciphered script show a highly organised society. Its origin and spread are best understood through its Early, Mature and Late Harappan phases.

1. Origin: two views

  • Diffusionist view: Mortimer Wheeler and Gordon Childe argued that the idea of city life came from Mesopotamia, pointing to trade contacts and some shared traits.
  • Indigenous evolution (now accepted): excavations at Mehrgarh in Baluchistan (J.-F. Jarrige) show farming villages from about 7000 BCE, with wheat, barley, cattle and mud-brick houses, growing step by step towards urban life.
  • Early Harappan phase (c. 3200–2600 BCE): sites such as Amri, Kot Diji, Kalibangan and Rehman Dheri already had fortifications, wheel-made pottery and planned layouts, the direct ancestors of the mature cities.
  • Distinctiveness: the script, seals, grid planning and covered drains have no Mesopotamian model, and the Rakhigarhi ancient-DNA study (2019) traced Harappan ancestry largely to local populations.

2. Expansion and extent

  • Area: the civilization covered about 1.3 million sq km, larger than ancient Egypt or Mesopotamia.
  • Core along rivers: major cities followed the Indus and the Ghaggar-Hakra — Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Ganweriwala, Rakhigarhi, Kalibangan and Banawali.
  • Coastal Gujarat: Lothal (with its dockyard), Dholavira (with its water reservoirs) and Surkotada linked the civilization to sea trade.
  • Frontiers: Manda in the north, Daimabad in the south, Sutkagen-dor in the west and Alamgirpur in the east; Shortughai in Afghanistan was a trading outpost.

3. Drivers of expansion

  • Fertile floodplains: farming of wheat and barley on river floodplains produced a surplus to feed cities, craftsmen and traders.
  • Trade and raw materials: copper from Khetri, lapis lazuli from Badakhshan, and shell and carnelian from Gujarat; Mesopotamian texts call the region "Meluhha".
  • Standardisation: bricks in the ratio 1:2:4, uniform weights and seals sustained a common economic system across distant regions.
  • Later shift: after about 1900 BCE, as rivers changed course and trade declined (the causes are debated), Late Harappan settlements moved east into the Ganga–Yamuna doab and south into Gujarat and Maharashtra.

AP angle: Andhra lay outside the Harappan zone; it was then home to Neolithic farming and cattle-herding communities of the southern Deccan, with remains at sites such as Nagarjunakonda.

The Harappan Civilization was thus an indigenous growth that expanded along rivers and trade routes. Ongoing work at Rakhigarhi and Dholavira (a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021) keeps refining this picture.
free.g1m-2025-p2-1b:
Shramana traditionFour Noble TruthsTriratnaAhimsa

In the 6th–5th centuries BCE, the Gangetic valley saw the growth of cities, trade and a shramana (ascetic) reaction against costly Vedic sacrifices, ritualism and Brahmanical dominance. Gautama Buddha and Vardhamana Mahavira, the 24th Jain Tirthankara, gave this protest its most lasting form. Both offered liberation through ethical conduct rather than ritual, and both preached in the people's languages, Pali and Ardhamagadhi.

1. Teachings of Buddha

  • Four Noble Truths: life is full of suffering (dukkha); desire (tanha) is its cause; suffering can end; and the way to end it is the Eightfold Path.
  • Ashtangika Marga (Middle Path): right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration, avoiding both luxury and harsh austerity.
  • Philosophy: dependent origination (pratityasamutpada), impermanence (anicca) and no permanent soul (anatta); karma decides rebirth, and the goal is nirvana.
  • Social message: silent on God; rejected Vedic authority, animal sacrifice and caste; opened the sangha to all, including women.

2. Teachings of Mahavira

  • Triratna: right faith, right knowledge and right conduct lead to liberation (kaivalya) from the cycle of birth.
  • Five vows: ahimsa, satya, asteya and aparigraha came from Parshvanatha, and Mahavira added brahmacharya; monks keep them strictly as mahavratas, lay followers as milder anuvratas.
  • Soul in everything: even stones, plants and water have a soul (jiva); hence extreme non-violence, fasting and austerity.
  • Anekantavada and syadvada: truth has many sides and can be stated only conditionally, a philosophy of tolerance.
  • Attitude to authority: rejected the Vedas and a creator God, but criticised varna less sharply than Buddhism.

3. Analysis: common ground and differences

  • Common ground: both were Kshatriya teachers who rejected ritualism, Vedic authority and priestly monopoly, and stressed karma, rebirth and moral conduct.
  • Differences: Buddha's Middle Path was practical, while Mahavira demanded rigorous austerity; Buddhism denied a permanent soul, Jainism saw souls everywhere.
  • Spread: Buddhism's missionary sangha and royal patronage (Ashoka) made it a world religion; Jainism's rigour kept it smaller but enduring among merchants.
  • Social appeal: both attracted the new merchant class, and their ethics of non-violence suited trade and settled farming.

AP angle: Buddhism flourished at Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda and Bhattiprolu, and Acharya Nagarjuna developed the Madhyamika philosophy; Jain remains survive at Ramatheertham (Vizianagaram) and Danavulapadu (YSR Kadapa).

Their message of ahimsa, tolerance and self-discipline inspired Ashoka's dhamma and Gandhi's satyagraha, and it remains relevant in an age of conflict and excessive consumption.
free.g1m-2020-p3-1a:
Constituent AssemblyCabinet Mission PlanBag of borrowingsConstitutionalism

The idea of a Constituent Assembly was first put forward by M.N. Roy (1934); the Congress officially demanded one in 1935, and the British accepted the demand in principle in the August Offer (1940). The Assembly was finally constituted in November 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan. In just under three years it framed the Constitution, adopted on 26 November 1949, whose merits and flaws have been debated ever since.

1. Formation of the Constituent Assembly

  • Strength: a total of 389 seats: 296 for British India (292 from the eleven governors' provinces and 4 from the chief commissioners' provinces) and 93 for the princely states.
  • Allocation: seats were shared among the provinces and princely states roughly in proportion to population (about one seat per ten lakh people) and divided among the General, Muslim and Sikh communities.
  • Indirect election: members of the provincial assemblies elected the representatives by proportional representation through the single transferable vote in July–August 1946. The Congress won 208 seats, the Muslim League 73 and small groups and independents 15; princely-state members were to be nominated by the rulers.
  • Working: it first met on 9 December 1946 (the League boycotted it), elected Dr Rajendra Prasad President and set up the Drafting Committee under Dr B.R. Ambedkar on 29 August 1947. After Partition its strength fell to 299.
  • Andhra members: Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar (Drafting Committee), N.G. Ranga, Durgabai Deshmukh and Pattabhi Sitaramayya.

2. Strengths of the Constitution as framed

  • Democratic content: universal adult franchise from the very first general election, a bold step for a poor and largely non-literate new nation.
  • Rights with remedies: justiciable Fundamental Rights backed by Article 32, which Ambedkar called the "heart and soul" of the Constitution, and Directive Principles to guide a welfare state.
  • Social revolution: abolition of untouchability (Art 17) and safeguards for SCs, STs and minorities; Granville Austin called it "first and foremost a social document".
  • Balanced institutions: parliamentary government, an independent judiciary and a federation with a strong Centre suited to a newly partitioned country.

3. Criticisms and the counter-view

These criticisms are only partly valid. Decisions were taken by consensus and accommodation rather than by majority votes, and the drafts were openly debated clause by clause.

In conclusion, the Assembly's legitimacy rests less on how it was elected than on what it produced: a democratic, rights-based Constitution that has endured for over 75 years. As Ambedkar warned, its success depends on those who work it, that is, on constitutional morality.
free.g1m-2020-p3-1b:
Judicial reviewBasic structureArticle 13Separation of powers

Judicial review is the power of the courts to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders of both the Centre and the States, and to declare them void if they violate the Constitution. Born in Marbury v. Madison (USA, 1803), it rests in India on Articles 13, 32 and 226 (with Arts 131–136 and 245–246). It is part of the basic structure of the Constitution (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997), so even Parliament cannot take it away.

1. Justice S.S.M. Quadri's classification

Justice Syed Shah Mohamed Quadri classified judicial review into three categories:

  • Constitutional amendments: Parliament's amending power is wide but not unlimited; amendments that destroy core features such as judicial independence or free elections can be struck down.
  • Legislation: laws are tested against Part III and the division of powers; even Ninth Schedule laws placed there after 24 April 1973 are reviewable (I.R. Coelho, 2007).
  • Administrative action: executive decisions are tested for illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety and, increasingly, proportionality.

2. Scope of judicial review

  • Three grounds: a law or order can be struck down if it infringes Fundamental Rights, lies outside the competence of the authority that framed it, or is repugnant to any other constitutional provision.
  • Judicial doctrines: severability, eclipse, pith and substance, harmonious construction and colourable legislation guide the courts.
  • Narrower than in the USA: Article 21 uses "procedure established by law", not American "due process"; Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened it by requiring procedure to be "fair, just and reasonable".
  • Limits: courts show restraint on economic policy (BALCO, 2002) and political questions.

3. Importance of judicial review

  • Supremacy of the Constitution: every organ must act within constitutional limits, upholding the rule of law.
  • Guardian of rights: it makes Fundamental Rights enforceable against the State.
  • Federal balance: it settles Centre–State disputes (Art 131) and checked the misuse of Article 356 (S.R. Bommai, 1994).
  • Checks and balances: it prevents a legislative majority from overriding minority rights.

AP angle: In E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of AP (2004) the Supreme Court struck down AP's law sub-categorising Scheduled Castes; a seven-judge bench overruled it in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024), permitting sub-classification.

In conclusion, judicial review keeps every organ within constitutional limits; exercised with judicial restraint and respect for the separation of powers, it strengthens democracy rather than rivalling it.
free.g1m-2020-p3-2a:
Quasi-federalismUnion of StatesUnitary biasCooperative federalism

India is a federation with a strong Centre. Article 1 calls India a "Union of States", which, as Dr Ambedkar explained, means the federation is indestructible and no State can secede from it. K.C. Wheare described the Constitution as "quasi-federal". The framers deliberately tilted the balance towards the Centre, while keeping a dual polity with a constitutional division of powers.

1. Why a strong central government?

  • Partition and unity: once Partition was announced in June 1947, the Union Powers Committee under Nehru gave up the Cabinet Mission's weak-Centre scheme and recommended a strong Centre with residuary powers.
  • Integration of princely states: over 550 princely states had to be merged into the Union, which needed a firm central authority.
  • Diversity: vast linguistic, religious and regional diversity raised fears of fissiparous and secessionist tendencies.
  • Planned development: removing regional imbalances and building a national economy needed central coordination.
  • Security and legacy: the war in Kashmir (1947–48) and the administrative continuity of the Government of India Act, 1935.

2. Provisions that create a strong Centre

  • Territorial power (Art 3): Parliament can alter the area, boundaries or names of States by a simple majority; the State Legislature's views are not binding. The AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 was passed though the AP Legislative Assembly had rejected the draft Bill in January 2014.
  • Legislative dominance: the Union List is the largest, residuary powers lie with Parliament (Art 248) and Union law prevails in Concurrent List conflicts (Art 254). Parliament can also legislate on State subjects under Articles 249 (Rajya Sabha resolution), 250 (national emergency) and 253 (international agreements).
  • Administrative control: States must comply with Union laws and directions (Arts 256–257), and failure can attract Article 365. The Governor is appointed by the President (Art 155) and can reserve State Bills (Art 200).
  • Emergency provisions: Articles 352, 356 and 360 can make the system virtually unitary.
  • Financial dependence: the most buoyant taxes lie with the Centre, so States depend on Finance Commission devolution (Art 280) and grants (Arts 275, 282).
  • Unified institutions: single citizenship, an integrated judiciary, All-India Services (Art 312), the CAG and the Election Commission; most of the Constitution can be amended by Parliament alone.

3. The balance today

  • Judicial safeguards: S.R. Bommai (1994) declared federalism part of the basic structure and limited the misuse of Article 356.
  • Cooperative institutions: the GST Council (Art 279A), NITI Aayog (2015) and the Inter-State Council (Art 263) promote shared decision-making.

In conclusion, the strong Centre has kept India united through Partition, wars and reorganisation of States; the task now is to balance national unity with State autonomy through genuine cooperative federalism.
free.g1m-2020-p3-2b:
Article 194Collective privilegesIndividual privilegesBreach of privilege

Legislative privileges are special rights, immunities and exemptions enjoyed by the Houses of a State Legislature, their committees and members, without which they cannot perform their functions freely. They are provided by Article 194 (Article 105 for Parliament) and extend to persons entitled to speak in the House, such as ministers and the Advocate-General, but not to the Governor, though he is part of the legislature. As no law has yet codified them, they remain as they stood when the 44th Amendment (1978) came into force.

1. Collective privileges (of the House as a whole)

  • Control over publication: the House can publish its proceedings and prohibit others from doing so; Article 361A protects the media's substantially true reports of proceedings.
  • Internal autonomy: it makes its own rules (Art 208), can hold secret sittings, and courts cannot question the validity of its proceedings on grounds of irregular procedure (Art 212).
  • Penal power: it can punish members and outsiders for breach of privilege or contempt by admonition, reprimand or imprisonment, and members also by suspension or expulsion.
  • Information and inquiry: it must be told immediately of the arrest, detention, conviction or release of a member; it can summon witnesses and papers; and no one can be arrested within its precincts without the presiding officer's permission.

2. Individual privileges (of members)

  • Freedom of speech: absolute within the House, subject only to its rules and to Article 211, which bars discussion of a judge's conduct.
  • Freedom from arrest: only in civil cases, not in criminal cases or preventive detention.
  • Exemptions: from jury service and from attending court as a witness while the House is in session.

3. Judicial limits

  • M.S.M. Sharma (1959): privileges prevailed over the press's freedom of speech, but remain subject to Article 21.
  • Keshav Singh (1964): courts can examine the legality of a legislature's committal of a person for contempt.
  • Raja Ram Pal (2007) and Amarinder Singh (2010): expulsions are open to judicial review for illegality.
  • Sita Soren (2024): a seven-judge bench held that bribery by legislators is not protected by privilege.

AP angle: In Andhra Pradesh both the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council (revived in 2007) enjoy these privileges through their Committees of Privileges.

In conclusion, privileges protect the independence of the legislature, but uncodified powers can be used against critics and the press; codification would balance them with Fundamental Rights.
free.g1m-2020-p3-3a:
73rd and 74th AmendmentsDemocratic decentralisationEleventh and Twelfth SchedulesState Election Commission

The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts, 1992 gave constitutional status to rural and urban local bodies, giving effect to Article 40 (DPSP) and the idea of democratic decentralisation. The 73rd Amendment (Part IX, Arts 243–243O, Eleventh Schedule with 29 subjects) came into force on 24 April 1993, now National Panchayati Raj Day; the 74th (Part IXA, Arts 243P–243ZG, Twelfth Schedule with 18 subjects) on 1 June 1993.

1. Structure of local bodies

  • Three-tier panchayats: village, intermediate and district levels (Art 243B); States with a population below 20 lakh need not have the intermediate tier.
  • Three types of municipalities: nagar panchayats for areas in transition, municipal councils for smaller and municipal corporations for larger urban areas (Art 243Q).
  • Grassroots bodies: the Gram Sabha of all village voters (Art 243A), and ward committees in municipalities with three lakh or more people (Art 243S).

2. Elections and representation
