  • Direct elections: all seats are filled by direct election for a five-year term, with fresh elections within six months of dissolution; the minimum age is 21 years.
  • Reservation: seats for SCs and STs in proportion to population and at least one-third for women; in panchayats, chairpersons' posts are also reserved, while for municipalities this is left to State law.
  • State Election Commission (Arts 243K, 243ZA): conducts local elections independently of the State government.

3. Finances, functions and planning

  • State Finance Commission (Arts 243I, 243Y): set up every five years to recommend the sharing of State taxes and grants.
  • Functions: States may devolve the 29 Eleventh Schedule and 18 Twelfth Schedule subjects for planning "economic development and social justice".
  • Planning committees: District Planning Committees (Art 243ZD) and Metropolitan Planning Committees for areas with 10 lakh or more people (Art 243ZE).
  • Audit: accounts are audited as provided by State law.

4. Exemptions: Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram and the Scheduled and tribal areas are exempt; the PESA Act, 1996 extended Part IX to Fifth Schedule areas with stronger Gram Sabhas.

AP angle: The AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 implements the 73rd Amendment; AP reserves 50% of panchayat seats for women and notified PESA Rules in 2011.

In conclusion, the amendments created a third tier of democracy; their success depends on real devolution of the "3Fs": funds, functions and functionaries.
free.g1m-2020-p3-3b:
Constitutional headArticle 163 discretionArticle 200Centre–State link

The Governor is the constitutional head of the State and the link between the Union and the State (Arts 153–162). Appointed by the President (Art 155) for five years, he holds office during the President's pleasure (Art 156); he must be a citizen aged at least 35. Like the President, he acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Art 163), except where the Constitution allows him discretion.

1. Executive and legislative powers

  • Formal executive: all executive action is taken in his name (Art 166), and the Chief Minister must keep him informed (Art 167).
  • Part of the legislature: he summons and prorogues the House, addresses the first session of each year and can send messages to the House.
  • During President's Rule (Art 356): the Governor administers the State on behalf of the President, aided by advisers.
  • Ordinances (Art 213): when the legislature is not in session, he can issue ordinances, which lapse six weeks after it reassembles unless approved.

2. Assent to Bills (Art 200)

3. Discretionary and special powers

  • Constitutional discretion: reserving a Bill for the President, recommending President's Rule (Art 356) and seeking information from the Chief Minister.
  • Situational discretion: choosing a Chief Minister when no party has a clear majority, or dismissing a ministry that has lost the confidence of the Assembly.
  • Fifth Schedule: in Scheduled Areas he can make regulations and reports annually to the President. In AP this produced the AP Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation, 1959 (amended 1970), protecting tribal land.

4. Controversies and checks

  • Misuse of discretion: the dismissal of the N.T. Rama Rao ministry in AP (1984), reversed within a month, is a well-known example.
  • Judicial safeguards: the floor test is the only way to prove a majority (S.R. Bommai, 1994), and Governors cannot be removed arbitrarily (B.P. Singhal, 2010).
  • Commissions: the Sarkaria (1988) and Punchhi (2010) Commissions recommended non-partisan appointees and limits on the use of Article 356.
  • Assent delays: in November 2025, answering a Presidential Reference, a Constitution Bench held that courts cannot fix timelines for assent and there is no "deemed assent", but prolonged, unexplained inaction is open to limited judicial review.

In conclusion, the Governor should act as a non-partisan constitutional bridge, using discretion sparingly and in the spirit of cooperative federalism.
free.g1m-2020-p3-4a:
BicameralismMoney BillCollective responsibilityElectoral functions

Parliament is bicameral. The Lok Sabha, directly elected by the people, represents popular sovereignty; the Rajya Sabha, elected by the elected members of State Assemblies by proportional representation, represents the States and acts as a revising chamber. Andhra Pradesh sends 25 members to the Lok Sabha and 11 to the Rajya Sabha. Their powers are equal in most matters, but the Lok Sabha is supreme in money and in control of the executive.

1. Functions

  • Equal powers: ordinary Bills, constitutional amendments (Art 368), approval of emergencies, impeachment of the President and removal of judges.
  • Joint sitting: deadlocks on ordinary Bills go to a joint sitting (Art 108), where the larger Lok Sabha usually prevails.
  • Rajya Sabha's special powers: it can authorise Parliament to legislate on a State List subject (Art 249) and to create new All-India Services (Art 312), by a two-thirds majority.

2. Control over elections

  • Presidential election: elected members of both Houses join elected MLAs in the electoral college (Art 54); all MPs, including nominated ones, elect the Vice-President (Art 66).
  • Presiding officers: the Lok Sabha elects its Speaker and Deputy Speaker; the Rajya Sabha elects only its Deputy Chairman, as the Vice-President is its ex officio Chairman.
  • Election law: both Houses equally make election law under Article 327, such as the Representation of the People Acts.
  • Own electoral base: the Lok Sabha faces the people every five years and can be dissolved; the Rajya Sabha is a continuing House.

3. Powers exercised only by the Lok Sabha

  • Money Bills (Arts 109–110): they originate only in the Lok Sabha, and the Speaker's certificate is final.
  • Demands for Grants (Art 113): only the Lok Sabha votes on them.
  • Responsible government (Art 75(3)): the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible only to the Lok Sabha, which alone can pass a no-confidence motion.
  • Emergency check (Art 352): only the Lok Sabha can pass a resolution disapproving the continuation of a national emergency.

4. Reasons for the Lok Sabha's supremacy

  • Popular mandate: being directly elected, it embodies the principle of "no taxation without representation".
  • Westminster model: as in Britain, the government must command the confidence of the popular House.
  • Federal role of the Rajya Sabha: a revising chamber and a forum of the States, not a rival centre of power.

In conclusion, the two Houses combine the popular will with federal balance; the Rajya Sabha's role is to revise and deliberate, not to obstruct.
free.g1m-2020-p3-4b:
Salient featuresFederalism with unitary biasParliamentary governmentBasic structure

The Constitution of India, adopted on 26 November 1949 and in force from 26 January 1950, is the supreme law of the land. Dr Ambedkar described it as "workable, flexible and strong enough to hold the country together". It blends features borrowed from many constitutions with Indian needs; five salient features stand out.

1. Lengthiest written Constitution

  • Size: originally 395 articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules; now about 470 articles, 25 Parts and 12 Schedules.
  • Reasons: India's vast diversity, a single Constitution for the Centre and the States, special provisions for regions and groups, and the influence of the Government of India Act, 1935.

2. Blend of rigidity and flexibility

  • Three methods of amendment: some provisions, such as creating new States (Arts 3–4), need only a simple majority, as with Andhra State (1953) and Andhra Pradesh (1956); most need a special majority (Art 368).
  • Federal provisions: these also need ratification by half the States, as with GST (101st Amendment, 2016).
  • Limit on amendment: the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) protects core features.

3. Federal system with a unitary bias

  • Federal features: two levels of government, a division of powers in the Seventh Schedule, a written Constitution and an independent judiciary.
  • Unitary features: a strong Centre, single citizenship, All-India Services and emergency provisions. The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) added a third tier.

4. Parliamentary form of government

  • Nominal and real executive: on the Westminster model, the President and the Governors are nominal heads, while the Council of Ministers is the real executive.
  • Collective responsibility: ministers are responsible to the lower House (Arts 75, 164), and the Prime Minister or Chief Minister leads the government.

5. Rights, Directives and Duties

  • Fundamental Rights (Part III): justiciable and enforceable through Article 32.
  • Directive Principles (Part IV): non-justiciable but "fundamental in the governance of the country" (Art 37).
  • Fundamental Duties (Art 51A): eleven, added by the 42nd (1976) and 86th (2002) Amendments.
  • Harmony: Minerva Mills (1980) held the balance between Parts III and IV to be part of the basic structure.

Other features include universal adult franchise (voting age lowered to 18 by the 61st Amendment, 1988), secularism, an integrated judiciary and independent bodies such as the Election Commission and the CAG.

In conclusion, these features make the Constitution a living document: borrowed in form but Indian in spirit, it has held a diverse nation together through constitutional democracy.
free.g1m-2020-p3-5a:
Judicial activismPIL and SALLocus standiJudicial overreach

Judicial activism is the proactive role of the judiciary in protecting rights and promoting justice, compelling the other organs to perform their constitutional duties. The term was coined by Arthur Schlesinger Jr. (USA, 1947); in India it grew from the late 1970s through Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer and P.N. Bhagwati, mainly through Public Interest Litigation (PIL).

1. PIL and SAL

  • Relaxed locus standi: any public-spirited person can approach the court on behalf of those who cannot, such as the poor and prisoners (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979; S.P. Gupta, 1981).
  • Epistolary jurisdiction: even letters and newspaper reports are treated as writ petitions, as in letters from prisoners about custodial torture.
  • New remedies: court-appointed commissions, continuing mandamus and compensation for violation of rights.
  • Constitutional basis: the writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226, the power to do "complete justice" (Art 142) and a wide reading of Article 21 after Maneka Gandhi (1978) gave courts the tools.
  • Social Action Litigation: Prof. Upendra Baxi called it SAL because, unlike American PIL, it seeks social justice for the poor and deprived.

2. Positive impact on the political system

  • Accountability: continuing mandamus in Vineet Narain kept investigating agencies under judicial watch, insulating them from political pressure.
  • Cleaner politics: disclosure of candidates' criminal, financial and educational records gave voters informed choices.
  • Rights and welfare: the right-to-food orders made cooked mid-day meals universal, served in AP today as Dokka Seethamma Madhyahna Badi Bhojanam.
  • Federal balance: Bommai made the floor test compulsory and checked arbitrary dismissal of State governments.

3. Concerns

  • Judicial overreach: strains the separation of powers, as in the friction over the NJAC verdict (2015); in the Aravali Golf Course case the Supreme Court itself warned judges not to try to run the government.
  • Lack of expertise and enforcement capacity: courts cannot monitor complex policies indefinitely.
  • Accountability gap: judges are not answerable to voters, so policy-making by courts raises questions of democratic legitimacy.
  • Misuse of PIL: frivolous "publicity" PILs add to pendency; State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010) laid down guidelines to curb them.

In conclusion, judicial activism has deepened democracy, rights and accountability, which justifies the statement; its legitimacy depends on judicial restraint and respect for the domain of the elected branches.
free.g1m-2020-p3-5b:
Gram SabhaPanchayati RajUrban local bodiesDevolution

The 73rd and 74th Amendment Acts, 1992 turned local bodies from creatures of State law into constitutionally mandated "institutions of self-government", giving effect to Article 40 (DPSP). Part IX deals with rural local governance (panchayats) and Part IXA with urban local governance (municipalities); both share common democratic features while reflecting the different needs of villages and towns.

1. Rural local governance (Part IX)

  • Gram Sabha: the assembly of all registered voters of a village is the base of direct democracy; it approves plans, selects beneficiaries and conducts social audits.
  • Three tiers: gram panchayat, intermediate (block or mandal) and district panchayat; all members are directly elected, while the chairpersons of the upper two tiers are elected indirectly.
  • Functions: plans for "economic development and social justice" on subjects such as agriculture, drinking water, primary education, health and poverty alleviation.
  • Tribal areas: PESA, 1996 gives Gram Sabhas in Fifth Schedule areas control over minor forest produce and protection against land alienation.

2. Urban local governance (Part IXA)

  • Three types: a nagar panchayat for an area in transition from rural to urban, a municipal council for a smaller and a municipal corporation for a larger urban area.
  • Functions: urban planning, water supply, public health, slum improvement and fire services (Art 243W).
  • Metropolitan planning: Metropolitan Planning Committees prepare development plans for large cities.
  • Finance: States may authorise municipalities to levy taxes, duties, tolls and fees (Art 243X), and the State Finance Commission reviews their finances.

3. Common features

  • Democratic base: direct elections, a five-year term and fresh elections within six months of dissolution.
  • Social inclusion: at least one-third of seats for women and SC/ST reservation in proportion to population.
  • Independent institutions: a State Election Commission and a State Finance Commission every five years.

4. Andhra Pradesh angle

  • Early start: AP was the second State after Rajasthan to adopt Panchayati Raj (1959), and in 1986 replaced panchayat samitis with Mandal Praja Parishads.
  • Present law: the AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 provides the three tiers below, and the AP Municipalities Act, 1965 governs towns.

5. Challenges: limited devolution of funds and staff, dependence on State grants, parallel bodies and delayed elections.

In conclusion, effective local governance needs genuine devolution of funds, functions and functionaries, timely elections and capacity building of elected representatives.
free.g1m-2020-p3-6a:
Public administrationPOSDCORBSteel frameCitizen-centric governance

Public administration is the organisation and management of the government machinery to implement public policy and deliver public services. Woodrow Wilson ("The Study of Administration", 1887) called it the "detailed and systematic execution of public law", and L.D. White defined it as all operations aimed at the fulfilment or enforcement of public policy. Luther Gulick's POSDCORB (1937) summed up its managerial tasks. In India it has evolved over two thousand years from royal administration to a constitutional, welfare-oriented system.

1. Nature of public administration

  • Integral and managerial views: the integral view includes all activities, from manual to managerial; the managerial view (Gulick, Simon) counts only planning, organising, directing and controlling.
  • Public character: unlike business, it works under political direction, the rule of law and public accountability, and must treat all citizens equally rather than seek profit.

2. Ancient and medieval period

  • Mauryan administration: Kautilya's Arthashastra described ministers, salaried adhyakshas (superintendents), a revenue system and espionage; Ashoka appointed dhamma-mahamattas for public welfare.
  • Local self-rule: Chola inscriptions at Uttaramerur describe elected village assemblies; the Guptas allowed greater provincial autonomy.
  • Medieval period: the Delhi Sultanate used the iqta system; the Mughals built a centralised structure of mansabdars, subas, sarkars and parganas, with Todar Mal's zabti revenue system.
  • South India: Vijayanagara had the nayankara system and ayagars (village functionaries); Krishnadevaraya's Amuktamalyada discusses statecraft.

3. British period

  • Civil service: Cornwallis, "father of civil services in India", organised the service; open competition for the ICS began in 1855 after the Macaulay Committee (1854).
  • District administration: the district collector became the pivot. Thomas Munro, Collector of the Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema), developed the ryotwari system.
  • Institutions: Ripon's resolution (1882) promoted local self-government, and the Government of India Acts of 1919 and 1935 provided for Public Service Commissions.

4. Post-independence period

  • Constitutional basis: Articles 308–323 provide for the services and Public Service Commissions; the All-India Services (Art 312) became Sardar Patel's "steel frame".
  • Development administration: the Planning Commission (1950) and the Community Development Programme (1952) turned administration towards development.
  • Reforms: two Administrative Reforms Commissions (1966, 2005), the RTI Act (2005), NITI Aayog (2015) and Mission Karmayogi (2020).
  • AP angle: village and ward secretariats (2019) and "Mana Mitra" WhatsApp governance (2025) show the shift to doorstep and digital delivery.

In conclusion, Indian administration has moved from a revenue-and-order state to a welfare and development state; its future lies in citizen-centric, accountable and technology-enabled governance.
free.g1m-2020-p3-6b:
ArthashastraSaptangaMansabdariZabti system

Kautilya's Arthashastra, attributed to the Mauryan period, is a normative treatise on statecraft, whereas Mughal administration (16th–18th centuries), shaped largely by Akbar, was a working system blending Persian, Turko-Mongol and Indian practices, described in Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari. Both were centralised monarchies run by a salaried bureaucracy, but they differed in the basis of kingship, the organisation of officials, revenue and control.

1. Basis of kingship and the state

  • Kautilya: the king is bound by dharma and his subjects' welfare ("in the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness"); the state is an organism of seven limbs (saptanga), and foreign policy follows the mandala theory and the six-fold policy (shadgunya).
  • Mughals: the Padshah was seen as divinely illuminated (farr-i-izadi, per Abul Fazl), and Akbar's policy of sulh-i-kul (peace with all) sought the loyalty of all communities.

2. Bureaucracy

  • Kautilya: a council of ministers (mantriparishad) and salaried adhyakshas heading departments such as trade, mines and agriculture; the samaharta collected revenue and the sannidhata kept the treasury. Officials were tested for loyalty by secret tests (upadhas).
  • Mughals: the diwan (finance), mir bakhshi (military), sadr-us-sudur (religious grants) and mir saman (karkhanas); officers were ranked by the mansabdari system (zat and sawar) and paid in cash or jagirs.

3. Revenue

  • Kautilya: usually one-sixth of the produce (bhaga), plus other taxes and state control of mines and trade.
  • Mughals: Todar Mal's zabti (dahsala) system assessed about one-third of the produce in cash, based on measured land and average yields.

4. Control, local administration and army

  • Kautilya: an elaborate espionage system, strict audit and forty listed ways of embezzlement; he warned that, like fish drinking water, officials may misappropriate revenue unseen. The gopa and sthanika supervised groups of villages.
  • Mughals: news-writers (waqia-navis) and frequent transfer of jagirs kept nobles in check; subas, sarkars, parganas and villages were run by subedars, faujdars, amils, muqaddams and patwaris.
  • Army: a standing army under the king (Kautilya) versus contingents maintained by mansabdars (Mughals).

AP angle: After Aurangzeb conquered Golconda (1687), Mughal revenue and mansabdari institutions spread over the Telugu country and were continued by the Asaf Jahi Nizams.

In conclusion, Kautilya's ideals of welfare and integrity remain relevant to modern public service, while Mughal revenue surveys influenced later British land settlements.
free.g1m-2020-p3-7a:
Development as FreedomCapability approachHuman developmentEnabling state

In "Development as Freedom" (1999), Prof. Amartya Sen (Nobel, 1998) defines development as "a process of expanding the real freedoms that people enjoy". It requires removing major sources of "unfreedom": poverty and tyranny, poor economic opportunities, systematic social deprivation, neglect of public facilities and repressive states. For Sen, freedom is both the primary end and the principal means of development.

1. Sen's idea of development

  • Capability approach: what matters is what people are actually able to do and be (their capabilities and functionings), not income alone.
  • Freedom as end and means: freedoms are valuable in themselves and also help people achieve other goals.
  • Agency: people are active agents of change, not passive recipients; Sen shows that women's education and agency reduce child mortality and fertility.
  • Example: Sen often cites Kerala, which achieved high life expectancy and literacy at a relatively low income through public action.

These freedoms reinforce one another; for example, free media and elections (political freedoms) help prevent famines, since governments facing elections and a free press cannot ignore starvation.

2. Characteristics of the new development thinking

  • People-centred: human development rather than GDP alone, measured by the Human Development Index (UNDP, 1990).
  • Participation and empowerment: decentralisation, self-help groups and people's voice in decisions.
  • Equity and inclusion: across gender, caste and region.
  • Sustainability: meeting present needs without harming future generations (Brundtland Report, 1987; SDGs, 2015).
  • Rights and institutions: a rights-based approach and good governance with strong institutions; state, market and civil society play complementary roles.

3. Four areas where the government has a crucial role

Drawing on the state's "fundamental tasks" in the World Bank's World Development Report 1997:

  • Basic education and health: these build capabilities and cannot be left to markets alone.
  • Social protection: food security (NFSA, 2013), employment guarantee (MGNREGA) and pensions for the vulnerable.
  • Rule of law and infrastructure: law and order, macroeconomic stability and public infrastructure let markets work.
  • Environment and regulation: protecting the commons and regulating markets to ensure equity.

AP angle: Thalliki Vandanam (2025) gives ₹15,000 a year for each school-going child, and the P4 (Public–Private–People Partnership) initiative, launched in March 2025 under the Swarna Andhra@2047 vision, links better-off families with the poorest to end poverty.

In conclusion, development in Sen's sense widens people's freedoms; the state should act as an enabler, building capabilities without replacing individual agency.
free.g1m-2020-p3-7b:
Permanent executiveSteel frameCivil societyParticipatory democracy

Democracy needs both a competent, neutral state machinery and an active citizenry. Civil services are the permanent executive that advises elected governments and implements their policies; NGOs are voluntary, non-profit bodies outside the state that voice citizens' concerns, deliver services and hold power to account. Together they link the ballot box to everyday governance.

1. Role of civil services

  • Continuity and stability: they provide continuity amid changing governments; Sardar Patel called the All-India Services the "steel frame".
  • Policy advice and implementation: they give expert advice to ministers and implement laws and schemes down to the village.
  • Rule of law and neutrality: they uphold constitutional values impartially, supported by Article 311 safeguards and the conduct rules.
  • Welfare and crisis management: they deliver welfare and lead disaster response, as in AP's handling of Cyclone Hudhud (2014).
  • Elections: district collectors serve as District Election Officers, conducting free and fair elections.
  • Impartial service: recruitment on merit by the UPSC and State PSCs lets officers treat all citizens equally, whichever party is in power.
  • Example: S.R. Sankaran, an AP-cadre IAS officer, is remembered for his work on bonded labour and SC/ST welfare.

2. Role of NGOs

  • Advocacy: the MKSS campaign in Rajasthan led to the RTI Act, 2005.
  • Watchdog: ADR's petitions secured disclosure of candidates' criminal and financial records; NGOs also support social audits.
  • Last-mile service delivery: the Rural Development Trust (Anantapur, 1969) works in health, education and drought relief.
  • Empowerment and social capital: SEWA and women's self-help groups give voice to the poor and to women.
  • Policy innovation: NGO experiments are often scaled up by government; MYRADA's self-help groups grew into NABARD's SHG–bank linkage programme (1992).

3. Challenges

  • Civil services: politicisation, red tape, frequent transfers and resistance to change.
  • NGOs: weak internal accountability, donor dependence and misuse of foreign funds, regulated under the FCRA, 2010.
  • Mutual distrust: officials may see NGOs as obstructive and NGOs may see officials as unresponsive; regular consultation bridges this gap.

4. Partnership: AP's Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty (SERP, 2000) shows how government and community institutions can together build strong women's SHG federations.

In conclusion, a healthy democracy needs an accountable, people-oriented civil service working in partnership with a responsible, transparent NGO sector.
free.g1m-2020-p3-8a:
Civil societyArticle 71 of the UN CharterMulti-stakeholder partnershipNGO registration

Civil society is the arena of voluntary collective action outside the family, the state and the market: NGOs, community groups, trade unions, professional and faith-based bodies. Article 71 of the UN Charter (1945) allows ECOSOC to consult NGOs, and thousands now hold consultative status. The Charter opens with "We the peoples", and the UN increasingly works with civil society to reach those whom governments alone cannot.

1. Why the UN partners with civil society

  • Grassroots reach and expertise: NGOs deliver humanitarian relief, health care and refugee support where the UN has little presence, for example the Red Cross movement.
  • Advocacy and norm-setting: the International Campaign to Ban Landmines led to the Ottawa Treaty (1997), and ICAN (Nobel Peace Prize 2017) to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.
  • Monitoring: NGOs track human rights treaties and the SDGs; SDG 17 calls for multi-stakeholder partnerships.
  • Legitimacy: civil society carries the voice of people beyond governments and makes global decisions more accountable.
  • Implementation partners: agencies such as UNICEF and the World Food Programme deliver much of their work through local NGOs.

2. Importance of civil society

  • Deepening democracy: it keeps citizens engaged between elections and holds the state and market accountable, as in the RTI movement and social audits.
  • Voice for the marginalised: it represents groups such as tribals, Dalits, women and workers whose concerns may otherwise be ignored.
  • Social capital: voluntary networks build trust and cooperation, which make democracy and markets work better.
  • Service delivery: it complements the state in health, education and disaster response; in Andhra Pradesh, women's SHG federations and the Rural Development Trust (Anantapur) show this role.

3. Acts under which NGOs are registered in India

  • Societies and trusts: most NGOs register as societies or trusts, which are simple and low-cost forms.
  • Section 8 companies: offer stronger governance and are preferred by larger NGOs (formerly Section 25 of the 1956 Act).
  • Additional requirements: NGOs receiving foreign contributions must register under the FCRA, and those seeking government grants must enrol on NITI Aayog's NGO Darpan portal.
  • Tighter regulation: the 2020 amendment to the FCRA banned the transfer of foreign funds to other organisations and capped administrative expenses at 20%.

In conclusion, a partnership among the state, the UN and an accountable civil society is vital for inclusive, sustainable development.
free.g1m-2020-p3-8b:
Right to InformationArticle 19(1)(a)Public authorityInformation Commission

Right to Information (RTI) is the citizens' right to access information held by or under the control of public authorities. The RTI Act, 2005 (in force from 12 October 2005), born of the MKSS movement in Rajasthan, replaced the never-notified Freedom of Information Act, 2002. It aims at transparency and accountability, treating the citizen as the real owner of public information.

1. Rights available under the RTI Act

  • Right to information (Section 2(j)): to inspect works, documents and records; take notes, extracts or certified copies; take certified samples of material; and obtain information in electronic form.
  • Time-bound reply: within 30 days, or 48 hours if life or liberty is involved; information is free if the deadline is missed, no reasons need be given and BPL applicants pay no fee.
  • Right to appeal: first to a senior officer in the department and then to the Central or State Information Commission (Sections 18–19), such as the AP State Information Commission.
  • Proactive disclosure (Section 4): public authorities must publish details of their functions, budgets, officers and decisions on their own.
  • Narrow exemptions: only those listed in Sections 8 and 9; even exempt information can be disclosed if the public interest outweighs the harm (Section 8(2)).

2. If RTI is a Fundamental Right, why do we need an Act?

The Supreme Court has read the right to know into Article 19(1)(a): State of UP v. Raj Narain (1975), S.P. Gupta (1981) and Union of India v. ADR (2002). Yet a law is needed because:

  • An abstract right: a judicially recognised right is enforceable only through costly, slow writ petitions under Articles 32 and 226.
  • Machinery: the Act creates Public Information Officers, time limits, fees, appeals and Information Commissions, making the right quick and cheap.
  • Defined limits: it spells out "reasonable restrictions" (Art 19(2)) through specific exemptions, balancing transparency with security and privacy.
  • Positive duties: Fundamental Rights mainly restrain the State, while information access needs duties of record-keeping, disclosure and penalties.
  • Wider reach: the Act covers bodies substantially financed by government, and the Supreme Court held the Chief Justice's office to be a public authority (Subhash Chandra Agarwal, 2019).

3. Concerns

  • Autonomy: the RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 lets the Centre fix the tenure and salaries of Information Commissioners.
  • Privacy exemption: the DPDP Act, 2023 changed Section 8(1)(j) to exempt personal information more widely, raising fears of dilution.
  • Implementation: vacancies and backlogs in commissions, and attacks on RTI activists.

In conclusion, RTI turns citizens into partners in participatory democracy; independent Information Commissions and proactive disclosure keep this right to know meaningful.
free.g1m-2020-p3-9a:
Statutory bodiesRegulatory authoritiesQuasi-judicial bodiesNatural justice

Statutory bodies are created by an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature, which defines their composition, powers and functions. They differ from constitutional bodies, created by the Constitution itself (like the Election Commission), and from executive bodies set up by a government resolution (like NITI Aayog). Quasi-judicial bodies, whether statutory or constitutional, also have the power to adjudicate like a court.

1. Work of statutory bodies, with examples

  • Regulation: SEBI (1992) for securities markets, TRAI (1997) for telecom and the CCI (Competition Act, 2002) for fair competition.
  • Protection of rights: the NHRC (Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993), the National Commission for Women (1990 Act) and the NCPCR (2005 Act).
  • Vigilance and anti-corruption: the CVC (2003 Act) and the Lokpal (2013 Act).
  • Disaster management: the NDMA (Disaster Management Act, 2005).
  • Andhra Pradesh: the AP State Human Rights Commission and the AP Electricity Regulatory Commission (1999, under the AP Electricity Reform Act, 1998).

Such bodies bring expertise, continuity and freedom from day-to-day political pressure, and they remain accountable through annual reports laid before the legislature.

2. Countries where they are set up

  • Universal institution: statutory bodies are found in almost every modern state.
  • Commonwealth democracies: they are especially common in the UK (e.g., Ofcom), Australia, Canada and New Zealand.
  • Asia: Singapore calls them "statutory boards", and Malaysia also uses them widely.
  • USA: similar "independent regulatory commissions", such as the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Federal Trade Commission.

3. Quasi-judicial bodies

These are non-court bodies empowered to adjudicate disputes, determine rights and impose penalties. They follow natural justice and court-like procedures but are not bound by strict rules of evidence or the Civil Procedure Code, offering speedy, expert and cheap justice.

  • National Green Tribunal (NGT Act, 2010): decides environmental disputes, aiming to dispose of cases within six months; appeals lie to the Supreme Court.
  • Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions (Consumer Protection Act, 2019): three tiers, at district, State and national levels, settle consumer complaints.
  • Other examples: the Central Administrative Tribunal (Art 323A) and Information Commissions; L. Chandra Kumar (1997) kept tribunal decisions open to High Court review.

In conclusion, such bodies make governance more specialised and accessible; they need autonomy, timely appointments and adequate staff to remain effective.
free.g1m-2020-p3-9b:
Social auditGram SabhaJan sunwaiSSAAT

Social audit is a process in which the people, especially the intended beneficiaries, verify the implementation of a programme by comparing official records with ground reality and discussing the findings publicly, usually in the Gram Sabha. Pioneered by the MKSS's jan sunwais (public hearings) in Rajasthan in the 1990s, it is mandatory under Section 17 of MGNREGA, 2005, and Section 28 of the National Food Security Act, 2013 provides for it in the PDS.

1. Objectives

  • Transparency: public disclosure of records such as muster rolls, bills, vouchers and beneficiary lists.
  • Accountability: implementing agencies answer directly to the people they serve.
  • Participation: beneficiaries take part in planning, monitoring and evaluation.
  • Verification: checking the quantity and quality of works and the eligibility of beneficiaries.
  • Grievance redressal: complaints are heard in public and corrective action is taken.

2. Advantages

  • Detects leakages: fake muster rolls, ghost beneficiaries and inflated bills are exposed, and misappropriated funds are recovered.
  • Deters corruption: the fear of public scrutiny improves the quality of public works and services.
  • Empowers the poor: it raises awareness of entitlements and strengthens the Gram Sabha as a forum of direct democracy.
  • Builds trust: it improves relations between citizens and government and gives feedback for better policy.

3. Andhra Pradesh model

  • Pioneer: AP pioneered state-supported social audits of the rural employment guarantee scheme from 2006.
  • Independent unit: it set up the Society for Social Audit, Accountability and Transparency (SSAAT, 2009), independent of the implementing department.
  • Method: village social auditors verify records door to door, and findings are read out at public hearings with officials present.
  • National spread: the MGNREGA Audit of Schemes Rules, 2011 require independent social audit units in every State; Meghalaya passed the first dedicated social audit law (2017).

4. Limitations

  • Weak follow-up: findings are often not acted upon, and recoveries are slow.
  • Elite capture and pressure: local elites may dominate hearings, and social auditors face threats.
  • Limited independence and coverage: where audit units depend on the implementing department, or cover only one scheme, audits lose credibility and reach.

In conclusion, social audit turns citizens from passive beneficiaries into active monitors; it should cover all major welfare schemes and be backed by prompt action on findings.
free.g1m-2020-p3-10a:
E-governanceSMART governanceDigital IndiaAccountability and legitimacy

E-governance is the use of information and communication technology to deliver services, exchange information and integrate government systems: G2C, G2B, G2G and G2E. The Second ARC's 11th Report (2008), "Promoting e-Governance: The SMART Way Forward", saw it as a route to SMART governance: Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive and Transparent.

1. Why India uses the e-governance strategy

  • Efficiency: services become faster, cheaper and available anytime and anywhere, cutting queues and paperwork.
  • Transparency and less corruption: removing intermediaries and discretion reduces leakages, as with Direct Benefit Transfer (2013).
  • Inclusion: Common Service Centres and mobile services take government to villages.
  • Data-driven governance: real-time dashboards help plan, monitor and review schemes.
  • Participation: platforms such as MyGov (2014) let citizens give feedback on policy.

2. Journey from vision to implementation

  • Foundations: NIC (1976) computerised government work, and the IT Act, 2000 made electronic records and digital signatures legally valid.
  • NeGP (2006): Mission Mode Projects backed by State Wide Area Networks, State Data Centres and Common Service Centres.
  • Digital India (2015): digital infrastructure as a utility, services on demand and digital empowerment; e-Kranti carried NeGP forward.
  • Platforms: the JAM trinity, DigiLocker, UMANG, GeM, UPI and CPGRAMS for grievances; the DPDP Act, 2023 protects personal data.
  • AP angle: Mee Seva (2011), the Real Time Governance Society and "Mana Mitra" WhatsApp governance, launched in January 2025 with 161 services and offering 1,126 services across 35 departments by July 2026.

3. An accountable, responsive and legitimate government

  • Accountable: the executive answers to the legislature daily through questions and committees, while the CAG, courts and RTI add independent scrutiny.
  • Responsive: grievance portals, service guarantees and real-time feedback make officials act within fixed timelines.
  • Legitimate: authority flows from the Constitution and regular elections; India's record of peaceful transfers of power after elections underlines this legitimacy.

4. Challenges

  • Digital divide: gaps in connectivity, devices and digital literacy, especially among rural women and the elderly, can exclude the very people e-governance aims to serve.
  • Exclusion errors: failures of biometric authentication or of servers can deny rations or pensions, so offline alternatives must remain.
  • Cyber security and privacy: large government databases attract attacks and need strong protection under the DPDP Act.

In conclusion, e-governance can deepen accountability and responsiveness, provided the digital divide, cyber security and data privacy are addressed.
free.g1m-2020-p3-10b:
Human capitalNational Health MissionRTE ActNEP 2020

The social sector, especially health and education, builds human capital, the foundation of growth and of the capabilities that Amartya Sen stresses. Public health is a State subject, while education was moved to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment (1976), so both the Centre and the States act. Their interventions are guided by Articles 21, 21A, 41, 45 and 47.

1. Health interventions

  • National Health Mission (NRHM 2005, NUHM 2013): ASHA workers, the Janani Suraksha Yojana for institutional deliveries, and free drugs and diagnostics.
  • Ayushman Bharat (2018): Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (formerly Health and Wellness Centres) provide primary care, and PM-JAY gives ₹5 lakh per family per year for hospital care, extended in 2024 to all citizens aged 70 and above.
  • Prevention and nutrition: Mission Indradhanush (2014) for immunisation and POSHAN Abhiyaan (2018) against malnutrition.
  • Digital health and policy: the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (2021); the National Health Policy, 2017 targeted public health spending of 2.5% of GDP by 2025.

2. Education interventions

  • RTE Act, 2009 (Art 21A, 86th Amendment): free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14, with 25% of entry-level seats in private schools for disadvantaged children.
  • Samagra Shiksha (2018): an integrated scheme from pre-school to Class 12.
  • Nutrition and learning: PM POSHAN (2021, formerly the Mid-Day Meal Scheme), NIPUN Bharat (2021) for foundational literacy and numeracy, and PM SHRI schools (2022).
  • Inclusion: scholarships for SC, ST, OBC and minority students, and Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas (residential schools for girls from disadvantaged groups).
  • NEP 2020: a 5+3+3+4 structure, mother-tongue instruction in the early years and public spending of 6% of GDP.

3. Andhra Pradesh angle

  • Health: Dr NTR Vaidya Seva (formerly Dr YSR Aarogyasri) provides cashless treatment.
  • Education: Thalliki Vandanam (2025, replacing Amma Vodi) gives ₹15,000 a year per school-going child from Class 1 to Intermediate (₹2,000 of it for school upkeep); the Dokka Seethamma mid-day meal was extended to 475 government junior colleges in January 2025; Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan Vidyarthi Mitra provides school kits.

4. Gaps

  • Health: low public spending and high out-of-pocket costs, and shortages of doctors in rural areas.
  • Education: poor learning outcomes, teacher vacancies and dropouts at the secondary level.

In conclusion, higher public spending, a focus on outcomes rather than outlays, and Centre–State convergence are the way forward.
free.g1m-2020-p3-11a:
EthicsDharmaEthics infrastructureNolan principles

Ethics (from the Greek "ethos", character) is the branch of moral philosophy that studies right and wrong conduct, good and bad, and duty. It provides standards to judge actions and guide choices in private and public life. In public service, ethics means using entrusted power only for the public good. India's tradition offers a rich store of such ideas, from dharma to Gandhi's purity of means.

1. Ethics in Indian tradition

  • Vedic roots: rta (cosmic order) and satya (truth) were seen as the moral foundation of the universe and of human conduct.
  • Dharma and purusharthas: dharma, duty suited to one's role, regulates the pursuit of artha (wealth) and kama (desire), with moksha as the final goal.
  • Bhagavad Gita: nishkama karma (action without attachment to results) and lokasangraha (welfare of the world) suit a public servant's duty.
  • Buddhism and Jainism: the Eightfold Path and the middle way; ahimsa and anekantavada (respect for many viewpoints).
  • Statecraft and regional voices: Kautilya's raja-dharma ("in the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness"), Tiruvalluvar's Tirukkural, and in Telugu, Vemana's verses attacking hypocrisy and caste pride.
  • Gandhi: purity of means, trusteeship and his talisman: recall the face of the poorest person before taking a decision.

2. Five principles to manage ethics in public service

Drawn from the OECD's Principles for Managing Ethics in the Public Service (1998):

  • Clear standards: officials must know what is expected of them, including rules on gifts, assets and conflicts of interest.
  • Legal framework: laws define offences and penalties, so that ethics is backed by enforceable rules.
  • Transparency: decisions open to public scrutiny leave less room for arbitrariness and corruption.
  • Accountability: effective inquiry and sanction show that misconduct has consequences, while honest whistle-blowers are protected.
  • Leadership and training: the conduct of senior officers and regular ethics training shape the culture of an organisation more than rules alone.

3. Complementary principles: the Nolan Committee's seven principles of public life (UK, 1995), namely selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty and leadership, point the same way.

AP angle: Vemana's verses on honesty and the AP Anti-Corruption Bureau's work show that ethical ideals and enforcement must go together.

In conclusion, blending India's heritage of dharma and seva with modern institutional safeguards can build a public service that is both efficient and upright.
free.g1m-2020-p3-11b:
Labour CodesFlexicuritySocial securityGig workers

Labour laws regulate the relationship among employers, workers and the State. Labour is in the Concurrent List, and Articles 23, 24, 39, 41, 42, 43 and 43A direct the State to secure just and humane conditions of work, a living wage and workers' participation in management. On 21 November 2025, four Labour Codes (Wages; Industrial Relations; Social Security; Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions) came into force, replacing 29 central laws.

1. Necessity and importance of labour laws

  • Unequal bargaining power: an individual worker cannot negotiate as an equal with an employer, so law must prevent exploitation, forced labour and child labour (Arts 23, 24).
  • Decent work: minimum wages, safe working conditions, social security and the right to form unions (Art 19(1)(c)).
  • Industrial peace: machinery for settling disputes keeps production, investment and employment going.
  • Protecting the informal sector: most Indian workers are informal and need a basic floor of protection.
  • Simplification: the Second National Commission on Labour (2002) recommended grouping the many laws into a few codes, which also eases compliance.

2. Gains for employers (factories)

  • Flexibility: government permission for layoff, retrenchment and closure is needed only in establishments with 300 or more workers (earlier 100); standing orders also apply only from 300.
  • Ease of compliance: fixed-term employment, single registration and return, inspector-cum-facilitators, decriminalisation of minor offences and higher factory thresholds.
  • Criticism: trade unions see these as diluting job security and curbing strikes.

3. Gains for workers

  • Wages: statutory minimum wages for all workers, a national floor wage and timely payment of wages.
  • Social security: gig and platform workers are covered for the first time, with aggregators contributing 1–2% of annual turnover (capped at 5% of payments to such workers); ESIC coverage widens.
  • Job security and welfare: gratuity for fixed-term employees after one year, mandatory appointment letters, night shifts for women with consent and safeguards, free annual health check-ups and a reskilling fund for retrenched workers.

4. Assessment

  • Not merely a gift to factories: the Codes aim at "flexicurity", flexibility for enterprises with security for workers.
  • Real test: benefits depend on enforcement, on funding of social-security schemes and on the registration of informal and gig workers.
  • AP angle: as labour is a concurrent subject, actual benefits in States like Andhra Pradesh depend on State rules and their enforcement.

In conclusion, the Codes can promote both ease of doing business and decent work, if implemented in a spirit of tripartite dialogue among government, employers and unions.
free.g1m-2020-p3-12a:
ValuesValue educationGender inequalitySocial reform

Values are enduring beliefs about what is good and desirable that guide choices and behaviour. The values of an entity, whether an individual, a family, an organisation or a nation, are the core principles that define its identity and conduct; for example, the Preamble commits India to justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. How society came to see gender inequality as injustice shows how values change.

1. Values of an entity

  • Individual: honesty, compassion and courage shape personal character.
  • Organisation: values such as integrity, service and excellence guide the conduct of its members, as in a civil service code.
  • Nation: constitutional values such as secularism, democracy and social justice hold a diverse people together.

2. Need for value education

  • Character: Gandhi listed "knowledge without character" among the seven social sins; education must build ethical judgement, not only skills.
  • Citizenship and cohesion: it builds constitutional values, respect for diversity and Fundamental Duties, as NEP 2020 stresses.
  • Countering social evils: it challenges prejudice, corruption, violence and gender bias from childhood.

3. How gender inequality came to be recognised

  • Accepted as tradition: sati, child marriage, enforced widowhood and denial of education were long accepted as custom.
  • Reformers redefined them as injustice: in Andhra, Veeresalingam organised widow remarriages and Gurajada Apparao's play Kanyasulkam exposed bride-price.
  • National movement and Constitution: women entered public life, and the Constitution guaranteed equality.
  • Women's movement: the "Towards Equality" report revealed a declining sex ratio and women's marginalisation, sparking campaigns against dowry and custodial rape (Mathura case).

4. Responses this recognition produced

  • Laws: the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, Section 498A IPC (1983; now Sections 85–86 BNS), the PCPNDT Act, 1994, the Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and the POSH Act, 2013.
  • Institutions and policies: the National Commission for Women (1992), gender budgeting (2005–06) and Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015).
  • Political representation: one-third of seats for women in local bodies (1992) and in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies (106th Amendment, 2023), to take effect after delimitation.
  • AP angle: the Hindu Succession (AP Amendment) Act, 1986 gave daughters coparcenary rights, before the central 2005 amendment.

In conclusion, the recognition of gender inequality has moved from social reform to rights; value education must now make gender equality a lived value at home and in public life.
free.g1m-2020-p3-12b:
LokpalLokayuktaOmbudsmanAnti-corruption

The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (in force from 16 January 2014) created an independent anti-corruption ombudsman: the Lokpal for the Union and Lokayuktas for the States. The idea, inspired by the Scandinavian ombudsman, was recommended by the First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966), and the Act followed a mass anti-corruption movement in 2011.

1. Composition and appointment

  • Structure: a chairperson and up to eight members; half are judicial members, and at least half are from SCs, STs, OBCs, minorities and women.
  • Term: five years or until the age of 70.
  • Selection committee: the Prime Minister, the Lok Sabha Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, the Chief Justice of India or a nominated judge, and an eminent jurist; appointment is by the President.

2. Jurisdiction

  • Prime Minister: covered, except on international relations, security, public order, atomic energy and space; an inquiry needs the approval of two-thirds of the full bench and is held in camera.
  • Ministers, MPs and officials: all Group A, B, C and D officials of the Union.
  • Other bodies: officers of government-funded bodies and of societies and trusts receiving foreign donations above ₹10 lakh a year, for offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

3. Powers and procedure

  • Own wings: the Lokpal has its own Inquiry and Prosecution Wings and superintendence over the CBI in cases it refers.
  • Attachment of property: it can attach and confiscate property acquired by corrupt means.
  • Protection of honest officials: false and frivolous complaints are punishable.
  • Independence: the chairperson and members can be removed for misbehaviour only by the President after an inquiry by the Supreme Court, and they cannot be reappointed.

4. Lokayuktas

Section 63 required every State to set up a Lokayukta within a year, leaving its structure to State law. Andhra Pradesh already had its Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act, 1983.

5. Limitations

  • Delays: the first Lokpal was appointed only in 2019, five years after the Act came into force.
  • Few prosecutions: dependence on the CBI and other agencies for investigation.
  • Weak whistle-blower protection: complainants and witnesses remain vulnerable.

In conclusion, independent, well-staffed ombudsmen with timely appointments can make the Act a real deterrent to corruption.
free.g1m-2020-p3-13a:
Moral attitudeMoral convictionPolitical socialisationPolitical attitude

An attitude is a learned, relatively enduring positive or negative evaluation of a person, object or idea, with cognitive, affective and behavioural components. A moral attitude is an attitude rooted in convictions about right and wrong, for example "corruption is wrong" or "caste discrimination is unjust". Unlike ordinary preferences, moral attitudes are held with strong conviction and resist compromise.

1. Four qualities of moral attitude

Drawn from Linda Skitka's research on moral conviction:

  • Universality: a moral attitude is held to apply to all people, not as a personal or cultural preference.
  • Objectivity: it is perceived as a matter of fact, as true as an empirical fact.
  • Independence from authority: it is held even when laws, leaders or group norms say otherwise.
  • Emotional intensity: it arouses moral emotions such as indignation or guilt, drives action and resists compromise.

2. Moral attitude in administration

  • Integrity: strong moral attitudes help officers refuse bribes and resist unlawful orders.
  • Risk of rigidity: because moral convictions resist compromise, they can turn into intolerance of other views; empathy and dialogue are needed.
  • Attitudes can change: being learnt, they can be reshaped by persuasion, training and contact with diverse people.

3. Factors that shape political attitude

Political attitudes, such as trust in government, party loyalty or ideology, are formed through political socialisation.

  • Family: the first agent of political socialisation, passing on party loyalties and ideology.
  • Education and peer groups: develop critical thinking and expose people to debate and diverse views.
  • Mass and social media: set the agenda and frame issues, but can create echo chambers and spread misinformation.
  • Social identity: caste, religion, language, region and class influence political preferences.
  • Economic interests and personal experience: contact with welfare schemes, corruption or the police shapes trust in government.
  • Political events and leadership: movements, crises and charismatic leaders leave lasting imprints.
  • Political culture: Almond and Verba (1963) classified citizens' orientations as parochial, subject or participant, reflecting how far people see themselves as active in politics.

AP angle: Potti Sriramulu's fast (1952) and the formation of Andhra State (1953) shaped strong linguistic and regional political attitudes in the Telugu region.

In conclusion, democracy is strengthened when political attitudes rest on information and constitutional values rather than prejudice, which civic education and a responsible media can promote.
free.g1m-2020-p3-13b:
Emotional intelligenceAbility, trait and mixed modelsEmpathyHumane administration

Emotional intelligence (EI) is the ability to perceive, understand, use and manage one's own emotions and those of others. The term was introduced by Peter Salovey and John Mayer (1990) and popularised by Daniel Goleman's book "Emotional Intelligence" (1995), subtitled "Why It Can Matter More Than IQ". In administration, where officers deal with people under pressure every day, EI complements technical skill and integrity.

1. The concept

  • Self-related skills: recognising one's own emotions and regulating them, such as controlling anger or anxiety in a crisis.
  • Social skills: recognising others' emotions (empathy) and managing relationships, such as calming an agitated crowd.
  • Distinct from IQ: EI concerns how well a person uses emotions in thinking and behaviour, and it can be learnt.
  • Example: an officer who listens patiently to a farmer whose crop has failed, explains his entitlements and speeds up compensation builds trust in government.

2. Three main models of EI

  • Ability model (Mayer and Salovey): EI is a form of intelligence with four branches: perceiving emotions, using emotions to facilitate thought, understanding emotions and managing emotions. It is measured like IQ, by tests with right and wrong answers.
  • Trait model (K.V. Petrides): EI is a set of self-perceived emotional dispositions that are part of personality, measured by self-report questionnaires.
  • Mixed model (Daniel Goleman): combines abilities and personality traits into five competencies: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills. Reuven Bar-On's model is another mixed model.

3. Application in administration and governance

  • Leadership and teamwork: motivating staff, recognising stress and resolving conflicts within the office.
  • Citizen-centric service: empathy with the poor, the elderly and persons with disabilities at grievance meetings and service counters.
  • Crisis and disaster management: calm decision-making under pressure, as in cyclone relief in coastal Andhra Pradesh (Hudhud, 2014; Titli, 2018).
  • Conflict resolution and negotiation: handling protests, communal tension, land acquisition and the resettlement of project-displaced families with sensitivity.
  • Ethical decision-making: controlling anger, fear or temptation, and avoiding bias.
  • Political–executive relations: maintaining composure and professional relations under pressure.

4. Building EI: behavioural competencies are part of capacity building under Mission Karmayogi (2020), alongside mentoring, feedback and reflective practice.

In conclusion, EI complements IQ and technical skill; it can be developed through training and reflection, making administration more humane, responsive and effective.
free.g1m-2020-p3-14a:
Public servicePublic trustTrustworthiness and fortitudePreventive vigilance

Broadly, public service means any activity done in the public interest by a person holding public office or performing a public duty: government employees, elected representatives, judges, public sector employees and others paid from public funds, as the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 recognises in defining a "public servant". The guiding idea is that public office is a public trust, held on behalf of the people.

1. Trustworthiness in public service

  • Meaning: honesty, reliability, keeping promises, confidentiality and using public resources only for public purposes.
  • Confidentiality: guarding official information and citizens' personal data, as conduct rules require.
  • In practice: an officer declares conflicts of interest, refuses gifts, keeps records honest and delivers entitlements on time without bribes.
  • Example: Lal Bahadur Shastri resigned as Railway Minister (1956), owning moral responsibility for a rail accident.
  • AP example: S.R. Sankaran, an AP-cadre IAS officer, earned people's trust through simple living and commitment to SCs, STs and bonded labourers.

2. Fortitude in public service

  • Meaning: the moral courage and endurance to do what is right under pressure, threats or adversity.
  • Whistle-blowers: Satyendra Dubey, an NHAI engineer, exposed corruption in the Golden Quadrilateral project and was killed in 2003; S. Manjunath of Indian Oil was killed in 2005 for sealing a pump selling adulterated fuel.
  • Institutional courage: T.N. Seshan, as Chief Election Commissioner (1990–96), firmly enforced the Model Code of Conduct.
  • Everyday fortitude: an officer who refuses an illegal order or stands by a fair decision despite transfer threats.
  • Institutional support: the Government's whistle-blower resolution of 2004 (PIDPI), which made the CVC the designated agency after Dubey's murder, and the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 aim to protect those who expose corruption.

3. Three preventive measures against corruption

Robert Klitgaard's formula, Corruption = Monopoly + Discretion − Accountability, suggests where prevention should aim.

  • Reduce discretion through technology: DBT, e-procurement, GeM, online land records and single-window services remove face-to-face contact and middlemen.
  • Strengthen institutions and laws: Lokpal and Lokayuktas, the CVC and State Anti-Corruption Bureaux; the Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 2018 made bribe-giving an offence; whistle-blowers need protection.
  • Build an ethical culture: codes of conduct, value-based training (Mission Karmayogi), asset declarations, Citizens' Charters and social audit.

In conclusion, when trustworthiness and fortitude are backed by strong systems, public office becomes a genuine trust for the people.
free.g1m-2020-p3-14b:
SocialisationFamilyEducational institutionsValue inculcation

Values are learnt through socialisation: primary socialisation in the family and secondary socialisation through society and educational institutions. Together they shape a person's character, conscience and citizenship. A child first learns right and wrong at home, tests these lessons in school and among peers, and practises them in society throughout life.

1. Family: the first school of values

  • Role models: parents and elders model honesty, respect, compassion, discipline and sharing; children learn more from what they see than from what they are told.
  • Stories and habits: stories, rituals and daily routines teach right and wrong; Gandhi credited his mother Putlibai for his self-discipline and religious tolerance.
  • Changing family: joint families taught tolerance and care for elders, while nuclear families and screen time pose new challenges.
  • Correcting prejudice: the family can also pass on caste or gender prejudice, which must be consciously corrected.
  • Equality at home: when sons and daughters share household work and opportunities equally, children learn equality as a lived value.

2. Society: reinforcing and reforming values

  • Community norms: religion, festivals and peer groups reinforce cooperation, service and tolerance.
  • Reform movements: in Andhra, Kandukuri Veeresalingam championed widow remarriage and women's education, and Gurram Jashuva's poetry challenged untouchability.
  • Media and public figures: they act as role models; social media can spread both awareness and hatred.
  • Civic participation: volunteering, Gram Sabhas and community service teach responsibility towards others.

3. Educational institutions: systematic value formation

  • Curriculum: constitutional values, Fundamental Duties, ethics and the environment, as emphasised by NEP 2020.
  • Teachers as role models: Dr Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, Vice-Chancellor of Andhra University (1931–36), whose birthday is celebrated as Teachers' Day, and Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam inspired students towards service.
  • Co-curricular activities: NSS, NCC, sports and debates build teamwork, discipline and service.
  • Hidden curriculum: fair assessment, inclusive classrooms and respect for diversity teach by example.

4. Challenges: rote learning, commercialisation of education, weak role models, consumerism and digital distractions, and a gap between the values adults preach and the values they practise.

In conclusion, the three agents must work in harmony, through parent–teacher partnerships and community engagement, so that values learnt at home are reinforced in school and practised in society.
free.g1m-2020-p3-15a:
CybercrimeIT Act, 2000CERT-InData protection

Cybercrime is any unlawful act in which a computer, network or digital device is the tool, the target, or both. With rapid digitisation, UPI payments and cheap data, such crime is rising fast: NCRB's Crime in India 2024 (released May 2026) recorded 1,01,928 cybercrime cases, 17.9% more than in 2023, about 73% of them motivated by fraud.

1. Types of cybercrime

  • Against individuals: phishing and online financial fraud (UPI and OTP scams, fake "digital arrest" calls), identity theft, cyber stalking and bullying, sextortion, and morphed images and deepfakes.
  • Against property and organisations: hacking, ransomware, data breaches, denial-of-service attacks and theft of intellectual property.
  • Against society and the state: cyber terrorism and attacks on critical infrastructure (e.g., the ransomware attack on AIIMS Delhi, 2022), fake news inciting violence, child sexual abuse material and online radicalisation.

2. Importance of cyber laws in India

  • Legal base for the digital economy: the IT Act, 2000 recognises electronic records and digital signatures, enabling e-commerce and e-governance.
  • Defining offences: Sections 66 (hacking), 66C (identity theft), 66D (cheating by personation), 66E (privacy violation), 66F (cyber terrorism) and 67 (obscene content). Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Section 66A but upheld blocking under Section 69A.
  • Institutions: CERT-In (Section 70B), NCIIPC for critical infrastructure (Section 70A), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal and helpline 1930.
  • Privacy: after Puttaswamy (2017) recognised privacy as a Fundamental Right, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and its Rules (2025) regulate personal data.
  • Organised cybercrime: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 includes cyber-crimes within organised crime.
  • Evidence: the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 gives electronic and digital records the same legal effect as paper documents.

3. Gaps

  • Capacity: police need more trained cyber investigators and forensic laboratories.
  • Cross-border crime: many scams are run from abroad, needing international cooperation.
  • Awareness: low digital literacy makes first-time internet users easy targets.
  • Under-reporting: many victims, especially of sextortion, do not report out of shame or fear.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh Police run dedicated cyber crime police stations, and victims can report fraud quickly on helpline 1930.

In conclusion, cyber laws must keep pace with AI, deepfakes and cross-border crime, backed by skilled police, international cooperation and digital literacy.
free.g1m-2020-p3-15b:
Ethical relativismUniversalismConstitutional moralityChanging norms

Ethics are standards of right conduct. Core values such as truth, non-violence and human dignity are broadly universal, but their interpretation varies with time (historical period) and space (culture, region and context). This is the debate between ethical relativism and universalism, and it affects both private relationships (family, marriage, friendship) and public relationships (between officials, citizens and institutions).

1. Effect of time

  • Private relationships: marriage is now seen as a partnership of equals; adultery was decriminalised in Joseph Shine (2018) and consensual same-sex relations in Navtej Singh Johar (2018), and women in live-in relationships are protected under the Domestic Violence Act, 2005.
  • Public relationships: the secrecy of the Official Secrets Act, 1923 has given way to transparency under the RTI Act, 2005; patronage once tolerated is now a conflict of interest.
  • Gender roles: women flying fighter aircraft (since 2016) or working night shifts, once unthinkable, are now accepted, with safeguards.
  • New concerns: data privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017) and climate ethics show how technology and knowledge create new duties.

2. Effect of space

  • Private relationships: cross-cousin marriage (menarikam) is customary in Andhra Pradesh and much of South India but taboo in many North Indian communities; norms of dress, food, family hierarchy and gender roles differ between communities.
  • Public relationships: gifts to officials may be a courtesy in some cultures but are bribes under Indian conduct rules.
  • Global settings: diplomats and multinational firms must navigate differing norms on gifts, hierarchy and punctuality.
  • Role and context: role ethics differ for a doctor, a soldier or a judge; confidentiality binds a doctor, while a judge must give reasons in public.
  • AP example: the Devadasi (Jogini) practice, once locally accepted, was banned by the AP Devadasis (Prohibition of Dedication) Act, 1988.

3. Limits of relativism

  • Universal minimum: time and place cannot justify violations of human dignity; constitutional morality and human rights set a floor.
  • Against imposing one culture: recognising context also prevents one group from imposing its customs on others, so long as rights are respected.
  • Public servants: they must apply the law uniformly while remaining culturally sensitive, for instance respecting local customs in tribal areas without tolerating child marriage.

In conclusion, ethics evolve, but the direction of change should be towards greater justice, equality and compassion, guided by constitutional morality.
free.g1m-2023-p3-1a:
Article 19Reasonable restrictionsTest of reasonablenessProportionality

Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms to citizens: speech and expression, peaceful assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession, trade or business (the right to property was deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978). These freedoms are not absolute. Clauses (2) to (6) allow the State to impose "reasonable restrictions" by law on specified grounds, and the courts, applying the test of reasonableness, decide whether a restriction is valid. The aim is to balance individual liberty with social control.

1. Scope of reasonable restrictions

  • Only on listed grounds: each freedom has its own grounds (see table). In Kaushal Kishore (2023) a Constitution Bench held the grounds in Article 19(2) to be exhaustive, so no new ground can be added by invoking other rights.
  • Only by law: a restriction must be imposed by a valid law, not by an executive instruction (Bijoe Emmanuel, 1986, the national anthem case).
  • Grounds widened by amendment: after Romesh Thappar (1950), the First Amendment (1951) added public order, friendly relations with foreign States and incitement to an offence, and inserted the word "reasonable"; the 16th Amendment (1963) added sovereignty and integrity of India.
  • Special situations: Article 33 lets Parliament restrict the rights of the armed forces, and Article 358 suspends Article 19 during an Emergency declared on the ground of war or external aggression.

2. The test of reasonableness

  • No fixed standard (V.G. Row, 1952): the court weighs the nature of the right, the purpose of the restriction, the extent and urgency of the evil, proportionality and the prevailing conditions.
  • Not arbitrary or excessive (Chintaman Rao, 1950): a restriction that goes beyond what its object requires is unreasonable.
  • Substance and procedure: both the law and the procedure it lays down must be reasonable; Maneka Gandhi (1978) read Articles 14, 19 and 21 together.
  • Clarity: Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Section 66A of the IT Act as vague and overbroad, separating discussion and advocacy, which are protected, from incitement.

3. Proportionality: the modern test

  • Privacy: Puttaswamy (2017) adopted the test for the right to privacy, and the Aadhaar judgment (2018) applied it to uphold the scheme with limits.
  • Digital age: Anuradha Bhasin (2020) applied proportionality to internet shutdowns: they must be temporary, necessary, published and periodically reviewed.

AP angle: in the protective spirit of Article 19(5), the AP Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation (1 of 1959, amended 1970) bars the transfer of land in Scheduled Areas to non-tribals; in Samatha (1997) the Supreme Court held leases of such land to private mining firms void.

Reasonableness is thus a judicially tested balance: freedom remains the rule and restriction the exception, and proportionality ensures that the State uses the least intrusive means to protect the public interest.
free.g1m-2023-p3-1b:
Article 263Inter-State CouncilSarkaria CommissionCooperative federalism

India's federal system needs forums where the Union and the States can settle friction through dialogue. Article 263 empowers the President to establish an Inter-State Council (ISC), if public interest so requires, to inquire into and advise on disputes between States, investigate subjects of common interest to the Union and States, and recommend better coordination of policy and action. For four decades this provision was not used for a general forum, until the Sarkaria Commission pressed for one.

1. Genesis

  • A dormant provision: until 1990 Article 263 was used only for sectoral advisory bodies such as the Central Council of Health (1952).
  • Demand for a forum: the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966-70) and Tamil Nadu's Rajamannar Committee (1969) recommended a standing body for Centre-State consultation.
  • Sarkaria Commission (set up 1983, report 1988): recommended a permanent Inter-State Council under Article 263, which it called the Inter-Governmental Council.
  • Constitution: the ISC was set up by a Presidential Order on 28 May 1990; a Secretariat followed in 1991 and a Standing Committee under the Union Home Minister in 1996.

2. Composition and working

  • Members: the Prime Minister as Chairman, Chief Ministers of all States and of Union Territories with legislatures, Administrators of other UTs, and six Union Cabinet Ministers nominated by the Prime Minister.
  • Standing Committee: chaired by the Union Home Minister, with some Union Ministers and Chief Ministers, it prepares matters for the Council and follows up its recommendations.
  • Method: it is a recommendatory body; questions are decided by consensus, which suits a forum meant for trust-building.

3. Relevance for coordination and cooperation

  • Neutral platform: issues such as the Governor's role, use of central agencies, river waters, cesses and Centrally Sponsored Schemes need structured dialogue.
  • Policy review: it examined the Sarkaria recommendations and, at its 11th meeting (July 2016), the Punchhi Commission report.
  • Complement to other forums: it works alongside bodies with narrower mandates (see table).

4. Limitations

  • Advisory and irregular: it met only 11 times between 1990 and 2016, and follow-up on its recommendations has been weak.
  • Reform proposals: the Punchhi Commission urged at least three meetings a year to make it a vibrant forum.

AP angle: post-2014 issues between Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, such as the division of Schedule IX and X institutions and power dues, are discussed at the Southern Zonal Council and Union Home Ministry meetings; a regularly meeting ISC could settle such issues faster.

A permanent, regularly meeting ISC with a strong secretariat would turn cooperative federalism from a principle into a working habit of dialogue between the Union and the States.
free.g1m-2025-p3-1a:
Emergency provisionsArticle 352Article 356Federal to unitary shift

Part XVIII of the Constitution (Articles 352–360), drawn largely from the Government of India Act 1935, arms the Union with three kinds of emergency powers. They rest on the Union's duty under Article 355 to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance. During an emergency the federal system can turn almost unitary without any formal amendment.

1. Emergency functions of the Union

  • National Emergency (Art 352): proclaimed on war, external aggression or armed rebellion, only on the Union Cabinet's written advice (44th Amendment, 1978, which also replaced "internal disturbance"). It was proclaimed in 1962, 1971 and 1975.
  • President's Rule (Art 356): imposed when the constitutional machinery of a State fails, or when a State ignores Union directions (Art 365).
  • Financial Emergency (Art 360): when the financial stability or credit of India or any part of it is threatened; it has never been invoked.
  • Executive control: during a National Emergency the Union can direct a State on any matter (Art 353) and the President can modify the sharing of revenues (Art 354).

2. Impact on the legislative powers of Parliament

  • State List opens up (Art 250): Parliament can make laws on any State subject; such laws lapse six months after the emergency ends.
  • Longer life of the House: Parliament can extend the Lok Sabha's term by one year at a time (Art 83(2)), but not beyond six months after the emergency ends.
  • Rights-restricting laws: Art 19 is suspended during war or external aggression (Art 358), so Parliament can make laws that would otherwise violate it; enforcement of other rights, except Art 20 and 21, may be suspended (Art 359).
  • Ordinances: the President can issue ordinances even on State subjects when Parliament is not in session.

3. Impact on State Legislatures

  • Overridden, not suspended (Art 352): State Legislatures keep functioning, but their laws give way to Parliament's in case of conflict; an Assembly's term can also be extended (Art 172).
  • Suspended or dissolved (Art 356–357): under President's Rule, Parliament legislates for the State, passes its budget or delegates the power to the President; such laws continue until the State Legislature changes them.
  • Money Bills reserved (Art 360): in a Financial Emergency, State Money and Financial Bills may be reserved for the President.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh came under President's Rule in 1973, during the Jai Andhra agitation, and again in 2014 on the eve of bifurcation.

Safeguards: the 44th Amendment let the Lok Sabha end a National Emergency, and S.R. Bommai (1994) made President's Rule subject to judicial review and the floor test.

Emergency powers are a safety valve for national unity, but, as Dr Ambedkar hoped, Art 356 should remain a "dead letter"; the Sarkaria Commission's advice to use it only as a last resort keeps federalism intact.
free.g1m-2025-p3-1b:
Cooperative federalismArticles 256–257Union directionsArticle 365

The Constitution calls India a "Union of States" (Art 1). The Seventh Schedule gives States wide autonomy, yet the framers also placed definite constitutional duties on State Governments, so that 28 States act as parts of one nation rather than as rival units. Granville Austin called this blend of autonomy and obligation cooperative federalism; these duties are its legal backbone.

1. Administrative duties towards the Union

  • Compliance with Union laws (Art 256): a State must use its executive power to ensure that laws made by Parliament are obeyed; the Union may give directions for this. States' police and revenue staff enforce central laws such as the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the National Food Security Act.
  • Not impeding the Union (Art 257(1)): State executive power must not obstruct the Union's executive power.
